Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at Tyler Pounds Regional Airport Oct. 13, 2026, in Tyler, Texas. Vance is in Texas to campaign for Republican candidates on the November midterm ballot. (Saul Loeb/Pool/Getty Images)
100-SHOT SOMALI GANG GUN BATTLE ROCKS MINNESOTA AS SHERIFF WARNS 'WE'RE IN TROUBLE'

"If you elect Republicans, you may not agree with us on everything, but we agree on some basic principles," Vance continued. "Like, for example, everybody should be safe. Everybody should be secure in their communities, and we don't want let violent criminals come into our country.
"So, I do think that contrast is driven a little bit more starkly given what's happening in Minnesota."

Fox News Digital spoke with the vice president after a campaign rally in the town of Tyler, Texas, about 100 miles east of Dallas, Tuesday. There, Vance rallied for Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton who is also in a tight U.S. Senate race with Democrat state Rep. James Talarico.
FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON
The progressive candidate recently returned from a two-week campaign absence, which Vance described as "odd."

"How old is he? Thirty-five? Forty?" Vance asked about Talarico. "You've got to have the energy to do the job, and taking two weeks off the campaign in October — that's the meat of the campaign — I just think it's a very, very bizarre thing."
The vice president added that he hopes Talarico's health is OK but that Texans must weigh whether he has the energy to do the job as a U.S. Senator.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a campaign rally at the Cailloux Theater Aug. 31, 2026, in Kerrville, Texas. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
TALARICO DISAPPEARANCE HAS DEM VOLUNTEERS WORRYING AND TRUMP ASKING, 'WHAT IS GOING ON?'

In that race, Talarico has demanded a debate with Paxton, who has yet to oblige. President Donald Trump said the two should debate, posting to Truth Social that Paxton is "ready, willing, and able." Vance took a softer stance when asked about a potential debate.
"That's ultimately something Ken Paxton and James Talarico are going to decide," Vance told Fox News Digital, adding that Paxton will make a "great senator."

"Obviously, those are some … things the campaigns have to negotiate," he continued. "But I'll let Ken Paxton and James Talarico make that decision. Ultimately, they each have to make their case to the people of Texas."
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton during the Texas GOP convention in the George R. Brown Convention Center in Houston June 12, 2026.  (Melissa Phillip/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
Nationwide, Republicans are underwater when it comes to the economy and cost of living, along with the war in Iran, according to Fox News polling.
REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY.

Of those polled in September, 61% say gas prices are a major problem, up from 48% from two years ago, while 52% say the same for healthcare costs, up from 44%. Majorities also view housing costs (54%, down from 60%) and grocery prices (62%, down from 66%) as major problems ahead of the November election.
In a similar poll, 71% of respondents said the Trump administration lacks a concrete strategy for ending the ongoing war in Iran.
Gas prices have ticked up after Houthi-led attacks on a Saudi oil pipeline. (Aaron Schwartz/Reuters)
The two issues are closely related after gas prices spiked sharply from a national average of $2.98 per gallon at the start of the war earlier this year to an average of $4.33 per gallon today.

"Well, we obviously want gas prices to be as low as they possibly can," Vance said. "And I think voters have to ask themselves, ‘Who has affirmatively taken steps to lower gas prices in the face, of course, of the Iranians terrorizing international shipping?’"
REPUBLICAN LAWMAKERS BREAK WITH TRUMP ON DIESEL DEAL WITH RUSSIA
Vance accused Democrats of complaining about the problem without offering solutions.

"We saw the president's announcement, with Russian diesel being allowed to come into the market," he said. "We have massive refinery capacity that we're announcing that we're going to build upon here. So, we're doing everything that we can, recognizing that building out energy refining capacity takes some time.
"I'm very cognizant that a lot of Americans are struggling with high gas prices," he acknowledged. "We're doing as much as we can to address as much of the pain as possible."

The 50th vice president stopped short of providing a definitive end date or marker that would signify an end to the war but said Iran must commit "not to rebuild [uranium enrichment] capacity and to stay off a pathway of nuclear weapons."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"They're going to stay off the pathway that's developing a nuclear weapon, and I think the president's been quite clear about that. I think the entire administration has been quite clear about that."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Elon Musk blames Trump, US military for SpaceX restrictions Ukraine warns could have deadly consequences
summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX imposed a new speed limit on Starshield satellite service that Ukraine says is disrupting drone intercepts and military operations.
story: Draganfly CEO Cameron Chell says Russian mesh networks make drones harder to jam and far more precise.

Elon Musk pointed to the Trump administration Wednesday after Ukraine scrambled to reverse new Starshield restrictions put in place by the trillionaire's company that disrupted military operations and threatened Kyiv's ability to intercept Russian attack drones.

While Starshield is built and operated by Musk's company SpaceX, individual satellites and infrastructure are owned and controlled by the U.S. government — which he made clear in a post to X on Wednesday.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the SpaceX, Tesla and X CEO wrote in his post.

A source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital that Ukraine received no advance warning before the restrictions took effect overnight, despite relying on the service under arrangements contracted through the U.S. government until May 15, 2027.

Ukrainian forces discovered the change after experiencing connectivity problems and contacting SpaceX customer support. They were told Starshield service would be restricted on platforms traveling at speeds of 100 miles per hour or higher, the source said.
Musk did not say whether President Donald Trump, War Secretary Pete Hegseth or another U.S. official personally authorized the new restriction or explain why it was imposed.
The Starlink logo is displayed on a smartphone screen and a computer screen displaying a portrait of Elon Musk, the owner of Starlink. (Dominika Zarzycka/SOPA Images/LightRocket)
RUSSIA MAY BE USING HIDDEN 'LUNCHBOX-SIZE' DRONE DEVICES TO COUNTER UKRAINE DEFENSES: EXPERT
He also sought to distinguish the government-controlled Starshield service from SpaceX's commercial Starlink network, which he said cannot be used for offensive military operations.

The distinction comes amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Musk criticized Zelenskyy over those attacks days earlier, writing on X that the Ukrainian president had "gone too far."

Hours after the change was reported, Ukraine's former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said connectivity at speeds below the new threshold was being restored, while making clear that Kyiv was still seeking removal of the speed restriction itself.
"Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored," Fedorov wrote on X Wednesday. "Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense."
"Thank you, @elonmusk," Fedorov added. "We hope for your continued support."
An office building burns following a Russian drone attack in central Odesa, Ukraine, on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. (Michael Shtekel/AP)

Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, warned that the change could particularly hamper Ukraine’s efforts to intercept Russia’s newer, jet-powered Shahed attack drones, saying it threatened "one of our few chances to defend the country" against them.

Ukrainian forces have also begun documenting effects on the battlefield. Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps said one unmanned systems unit on the Huliaipole front had already been forced to cancel missions because of connectivity problems. The unit reported interruptions even while drones were traveling below the stated 100 mph threshold.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., pressed SpaceX for answers on X. "I'm confident this does not reflect a change in SpaceX policy because if so, intentionally degrading Ukraine's ability to defend itself might be construed as aiding and abetting a mass murderer. Can you confirm that's not SpaceX’s intent?"
Starshield is SpaceX's national security satellite service, based on technology developed for the company's better-known Starlink network.

The change could affect Ukrainian drones, aircraft and helicopters that rely on Starshield connectivity while moving at high speeds, including drones used to intercept Russian Shahed attacks. Ukrainian units had reported performance problems even at speeds below the stated threshold, according to the source.
UKRAINE SEEKS MORE US PATRIOT INTERCEPTORS AS BOMB SHELTER PROBE DEEPENS
President Donald Trump said he likes Elon Musk "a lot" after the pair faced a rift over the One Big Beautiful Bill earlier this year.  (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
Ukraine has contacted SpaceX seeking an explanation for the restrictions and asking the company to restore its previous service capabilities, the source familiar with the move told Fox News Digital.

They said Ukraine communicated to Musk's company that the restriction had not previously applied to its terminals and was creating significant operational problems for Ukrainian forces in its continued war with aggressor Russia.

Kyiv also noted that its current service arrangements, contracted through the U.S. government until May 15, 2027, cover land-based mobile and fixed uses, including mobile platforms, according to the source.
SpaceX had not responded to Ukraine’s request as of Wednesday morning, the source said.
PENTAGON CONSOLIDATES DRONE OVERSIGHT AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PUSHES RAPID UNMANNED WARFARE EXPANSION
Polish Foreign Minister Radislaw Sikorski tore into Musk over the restrictions.
"Hey @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, wea are watching you," he wrote on X.
Poland pays for more than 2,900 Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks at a press conference after meetings with the heads of the EU and Ireland following a formal ceremony to mark the launch of Ireland's eighth EU presidency, at Dublin Castle in Dublin on July 1, 2026. (Paul Faith / AFP via Getty Images)
Sikorski and Musk clashed last year over Ukraine’s dependence on Starlink, with Musk telling Sikorski, "Be quiet, small man."
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon, White House and SpaceX for details. There’s been no public confirmation that Musk personally ordered the restrictions.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Pentagon, through Space Force, contracts with SpaceX for Starshield services, giving the department a direct role in administering the government’s agreements with the company. But the existence of a Pentagon contract does not establish whether the military or SpaceX has authority over specific operational restrictions, including the new speed limit.

title: ‘Paid for the bullets’: Dem challenger hits senator with stunning ICE accusation during fiery Senate debate
summary: Troy Jackson accused Susan Collins of paying for the bullets that killed Johan Sebastián Guerrero, igniting a fierce clash over ICE funding.
story: Susan Collins, Troy Jackson clashed on Tuesday evening over views on whether ICE needs reform or abolishment after the death of Sebastián Durán Guerrero.

Fierce disagreement broke out on the debate stage on Tuesday evening as Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, defended her record against accusations that she had enabled the death of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Troy Jackson, her Democratic opponent, argued Collins had facilitated the deadly encounter on the three-month anniversary of the incident by funding what he described as a "rogue agency."

"Look, Senator Collins paid for the bullets and at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger," Jackson said, referring to the roughly $66 billion in funding for immigration enforcement agencies included in the Secure America Act, a party-line bill that extended provisions for the agency through the end of Trump’s term.
TRUMP TAKES ICE SHUTDOWNS OFF THE TABLE WITH SIGNATURE ON KEY $70B BILL
Former state Senator Troy Jackson, a Democrat from Maine and gubernatorial candidate, speaks during a Fighting Oligarchy event with Graham Platner. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"That's the choice on this stage. A senator who helps Donald Trump hurt Maine then tells us how concerned she is, or somebody who will stand up against him before another family in Maine has to pay the price."

Notably, not all of the funding described by Jackson was set aside for ICE. The package set aside $26 billion for border security operations under Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and $38.5 for ICE. The package also included $5 billion for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) general funds.

Guerrero’s shooting has become a flash point in Trump’s immigration enforcement push, especially in the Maine Senate race where Democrats have used his death to illustrate broader critiques of Collins: that her occasional willingness to break with the majority of the GOP hasn’t meaningfully curbed the administration’s policies. But at the debate on Tuesday evening, the third between Collins and Jackson, Collins pushed back on the narrative, arguing that her power as a Republican senator has been key to implementing a handful of safeguards on an agency that she described as critical to American safety.

"After the Biddeford shooting, I called the Secretary of Homeland Security, [and] met with the acting director and suggested that they prioritize Maine for receipt of these body-worn cameras. And they did. And every ICE agent in the state of Maine and across the country now has the body-worn cameras," Collins said at the debate on Tuesday.
"I increased by 17% the budget for the independent Office of Inspector General," Collins added.

Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian national, was fatally shot in Biddeford on July 13 when he tried to flee ICE officers in a vehicle during an operation targeting an illegal immigrant with a final order of removal, according to the Department of Homeland Security.
Guerrero was not the target of the operation.
'SQUAD' MEMBER CALLS DHS 'GREATEST THREAT TO OUR SAFETY' AFTER ICE-INVOLVED SHOOTING
Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Maine, is pictured alongside Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and, fearing for public safety, an officer discharged his weapon. The driver of the vehicle was struck and emergency services were immediately contacted. He passed away from his injuries," DHS said in a statement at the time.
In Jackson’s estimation, the moment is emblematic of what he described as an agency out of control.
"That is why I believe that this agency is just a rogue agency that's doing Donald Trump's bidding," Jackson said.
"I do believe it's important to get rid of it and take that money and prioritize it into existing law enforcement that actually people believe in."

Like many progressives, Jackson has argued that the agency is beyond the scope of reform, sharing the view of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The group, which backed Jackson in his gubernatorial bid earlier this year before he became a candidate for Senate, calls the agency "a violent and illegitimate agency."
Jackson has shared almost that exact framing, similarly stating that ICE "is not legitimate law enforcement," in a debate from last Thursday.
Collins disagrees.
On Tuesday, she argued that the agency, although flawed, serves an important role in American law enforcement, pointing out that its role overlaps with many other forms of law enforcement.

"It investigates child trafficking, human trafficking and general child exploitation: drug smuggling, international cartels, financial scams. It recently helped shut down a child pornography ring in the state of Maine. I don't think any of us wants to go back to the days of completely open, uncontrolled borders. That is dangerous for us," Collins argued.
EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET
Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine stands for an interview with Fox News Digital on Feb. 10, 2026 in Washington D.C. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think what happened is far too many ICE officers were hired and deployed without adequate vetting and training. But let us not forget the important work that ICE does, which is why it should be reformed and not abolished, as Troy has said."
Having secured their parties’ respective nominations, Collins and Jackson will face off in the state’s Nov. 3 general election.
Elaine Mallon contributed to this report.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: James Talarico torches Biden border policies in stunning attack ad as progressive tries to flip Texas blue
summary: James Talarico slams Joe Biden on border security in a new ad, but a 2019 interview shows he called to slash Texas' entire $800 million budget.
story: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico's campaign released an ad Monday that claims he scrutinized former President Joe Biden's border policies as "failing" Americans, despite an unearthed call to slash Texas' entire border security fund.

Texas Democrat candidate for U.S. Senate James Talarico appears to be further moderating his previous left-wing stances as he slammed former President Joe Biden for ‘failing us’ on border security in a new campaign advertisement released Monday.
Despite spewing a seemingly hawkish and downright right-leaning border stance in the recent ad, Talarico previously called to slash Texas’ entire border-security budget in an unearthed interview.
"I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border," Talarico says in the opening of the ad released this week.

But Talarico’s campaign couldn’t give Fox News Digital an example of him ever publicly criticizing Biden during his presidency. And the Texas Democrat explicitly made a call to put Texas’ entire $800 million two-year border security budget toward public education in a 2019 interview with The Austin Chronicle.
JAMES TALARICO ADMITS DEMOCRATS TOOK ‘BORDER FOR GRANTED’ UNDER BIDEN

Texas Senate candidate James Talarico slams former President Joe Biden in new campaign advertisement released on Monday, October 12. Texas Senate candidate James Talarico slams former President Joe Biden in new campaign advertisement released on Monday, October 12. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images; ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images)
"We're also sending about $800 million per biennium to the border with Mexico for ‘increased border security,’" Talarico said in the more than seven-year-old interview.

The two-year deal allocating $400 million per year toward border security in the state of Texas was the state’s entire budget toward warding off illegal immigration at the time Talarico made the call to replace that funding.
"I'd rather take that money and put it back into public education and help increase the basic allotment, for instance," he said in the interview.

Talarico has ramped up his efforts to come off more moderate amid claims that he is too progressive to win a Senate seat in notoriously red Texas. His move to a more moderate stance on immigration only started during his Senate bid in the state with the highest rates of illegal immigration.
"Putting a bunch of boats, planes and border patrol agents on the physical border is expensive and also does not solve the problem," he said in the interview.

His 2019 criticism of border enforcement comes to the surface as border crossings under the Trump administration fell to a new record low level in 55 years in 2025, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The decline in illegal immigration followed a series of immigration enforcement measures implemented by the administration.

"Everyone will admit it's just political grandstanding," Talarico said in the interview. "Certain lawmakers want to appease extreme parts of their base. And they do it by pumping money we don't have down to the border."
EXCLUSIVE: TALARICO CAUGHT ON TAPE GIGGLING ABOUT HIS CHURCH HOUSING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS SET FOR DEPORTATION

U.S. President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena in Clarksville, Tennessee on October 10, 2026. Trump is campaigning for Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm election. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)
In his run for Senate, Talarico has now labeled himself a "border security" Democrat, despite an extensive history of pushing back on border security reform and authorities.

A former member of the Texas legislature and a former school teacher, Talarico has been in the spotlight repeatedly for many of his far-left controversies, particularly comments regarding immigration enforcement. He has called to dismantle Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), claiming it was "time to tear down this secret police force."
Talarico also referred to illegal aliens as his "constituents."

He labeled Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s border security policies as "atrocities" and accused him of "hunting" illegal immigrants. The Senate candidate also said he "taught a lot of undocumented students," and that those illegal aliens were more patriotic than Americans.

"James is proud to be the only candidate in this race who has unveiled a border security agenda endorsed by Republican and Democratic border county sheriffs," Talarico's campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Fox News Digital when asked about the flip-flop.
TALARICO DISAPPEARANCE HAS DEM VOLUNTEERS WORRYING AND TRUMP ASKING, 'WHAT IS GOING ON?'

He continued, "James supports stronger border security and immigration enforcement — it’s why he’s called for more border patrol agents and has said we should be arresting and deporting violent criminals and human traffickers — not moms and babies."

The Texas Senate hopeful went briefly missing from the campaign trail this month, prompting viral rumors online to swirl that he was at a behavioral health center. Talarico debunked these claims after clearing the air on his whereabouts when he reappeared Friday, reassuring voters that he was recovering from the flu.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Talarico is running against GOP rival Ken Paxton for the Senate seat in Texas. The race has remained close as November’s midterms approach.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Dem senator's hiring announcement sparks GOP eruption over who is encouraged to apply: 'Blatantly illegal'
summary: Ed Markey's internship post encouraging BIPOC and LGBTQ+ applicants sparked accusations of discrimination and claims he violated civil rights law.
story: Incumbent Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., and Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., faced off over transgender athletes, ICE, socialism and term limits in their final debate before the Sept. 1 Democratic primary. (Credit: WCVB)
A Democratic senator is facing accusations of racial and sexual discrimination over a controversial social media post encouraging members of minority groups to apply for a role in his office.

"I’m hiring motivated and eager interns for the Spring 2027 semester in my Boston office. BIPOC, LGBTQ+, working class, veterans and other underrepresented candidates with Massachusetts ties are encouraged to apply," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., posted to X on Tuesday.
"Are white men allowed to apply, Senator?" Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, shot back on X Tuesday.
DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH
U.S. Rep. Brandon Gill (R-TX) looks on during a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing at the U.S. Capitol on March 26, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Getty Images)
Conservatives on X erupted with anger over the post, with some going as far as to claim the senator’s job posting was illegal.
"Crazy that a United States Senator can openly violate civil rights law on Twitter," conservative activist Chris Rufo wrote.
"This is blatantly illegal," Katie Miller, podcaster and wife of White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, wrote.
NEW YORK TIMES SUED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OVER ALLEGED 'DEI-RELATED' EMPLOYMENT DISCRIMINATION
Sen. Ed Markey, the more progressive of the two candidates, has the backing of Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Ayanna Pressley. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for MoveOn Civic Action)

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has stated in past guidance that encouraging applicants from certain backgrounds to apply for a job does not necessarily violate federal discrimination law. However, the agency also warns that job advertisements expressing preferences based on race, sex or other protected characteristics may be unlawful.
The Congressional Accountability Act also applies federal workplace discrimination protections to congressional offices.
The actual job posting on Markey’s Senate website does not bar White people from applying, despite questions raised by Gill and others about whether certain applicants were being favored.
Other conservatives stopped short of accusing Markey of breaking the law, but characterized his hiring practices as unjust nonetheless.

"You'll notice it's never ‘I'm resigning my Senate seat because white men have too much power’ or 'I'm donating my house to reduce the racial wealth gap,’" online commentator Bernard Stanford wrote. "That would at least be a personal decision. But no — the white male sacrificial burden is always foisted upon someone else."
DEMOCRATS’ GENERATIONAL BATTLE ERUPTS AS 80-YEAR-OLD SENATOR FACES YOUNGER CHALLENGER

SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler hit back at Democratic Sen. Ed Markey on Tuesday after he accused the SBA of raising a "Christian nationalist" flag over its headquarters to honor Flag Day. (Getty Images)
"Democrats will write stuff like this and then wonder why young white straight men have rejected their party in droves," journalist Corey Walker said.

"This is disturbing, especially from the Ranking Member of the Senate Small Business Committee," Small Business Administration Administrator Kelly Loeffler posted to her X account. "From day one we’ve said it: politicians need to stop picking winners and losers — and stop turning every government program into a DEI grift. America’s entrepreneurs compete on merit, not identity. That principle should be nonnegotiable for anyone entrusted with shaping our nation’s small business policy."

Markey’s office did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

title: Massive trove of Republican voter and donor info breached in Biden DOJ probe: Senate chairman
summary: Chuck Grassley alleges President Joe Biden's Justice Department collected invasive data on over 639,000 Republican voters and donors via Arctic Frost.
story: Fox News correspondent David Spunt reports on former special counsel Jack Smith testifying before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill as GOP senators press him on claims of political overreach.

FIRST ON FOX: A new memo obtained by Fox News Digital alleges that former President Joe Biden’s Justice Department collected information on hundreds of thousands of Republican voters and donors, including the names and home addresses of people who purchased red MAGA hats and Trump memorabilia.

The memo is part of an update from Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, and his investigation into former special counsel Jack Smith and his Arctic Frost probe, which was launched by Biden’s Department of Justice (DOJ) in 2022 to investigate efforts to overturn results of the 2020 election.
Grassley has been diving into Arctic Frost since last year, releasing a drip feed of whistleblower reports on the investigation that led to Smith testifying before the Judiciary Committee last month.
EXPLOSIVE NEW REPORT PUTS JACK SMITH BACK IN HOT SEAT AS JIM JORDAN ALLEGES HE TRIED TO 'SWAY' 2024 ELECTION
Former special counsel Jack Smith testifies during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in the Hart Senate Office Building on Sept. 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

The latest update found that Smith’s special counsel office and the DOJ "obtained spreadsheets containing Republican campaign donors, supporters, and detailed personal voter information in various formats, totaling over 639,000 individuals, at minimum," Grassley said in the memo.
"Out of those, over 148,000 rows are identified in the spreadsheets as donors," he continued. "The donors generally contributed small-dollar amounts."
Smith also sought and obtained information on the sales of red MAGA hats and Trump memorabilia, which Grassley noted included "individual purchasers and shipping addresses for home delivery."

"This is in addition to collecting a catalog of Trump campaign products including these red hats, T-shirts, mugs, and door mats," Grassley said. "This further illustrates the extensive scope of irrelevant and personally invasive records obtained by Smith which were shared with FBI agents."

The data gathered on the voters and donors included names, dates of birth, physical addresses, emails, whether the person was a registered Republican, their occupation and place of employment — samples on the list included retirees, pool technicians, drivers, loggers, etc. — credit card information, donor analysis data and donation amount, among other details.
JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS
Fox News Digital reached out to Smith’s newly launched law firm for comment.
The memo follows a previous release from Grassley that showed Smith’s team collected checks from nearly 5,000 Americans across the country who donated to Trump and Trump-aligned Republican entities.

"This update shows that Jack Smith and the Biden Justice Department collected incredibly invasive donor data — and voter data — beyond what could conceivably be necessary for him or his team to fulfill the [special counsel office’s] mandate," Grassley said.
HOUSE VOTES TO REPEAL CONTROVERSIAL ARCTIC FROST PROVISION FROM GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BILL

Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, speaks about the Arctic Frost investigation during a press conference on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., Oct. 6, 2025. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

"This update further corroborates that Smith and his partisan team aimed to map out the entire Republican Party apparatus," he continued. "I again call on my Democratic colleagues to join my oversight work instead of trying to defend Smith and sweep his abuse of authority under the rug."
Grassley noted that during Smith’s hearing last month, he pressed the former special counsel for a "yes or no" answer on whether his investigation gathered data on donors.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Yes," Smith said. "We acquired financial information. As I sit here right now, I cannot recite to you every subpoena we issued. I can tell you why we issued subpoenas. And it was to conduct a criminal investigation of one of the most serious crimes that's ever happened in our nation's history. I had a duty to collect facts."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Iowa Dem Senate candidate says he's too busy campaigning to attend all state House votes
summary: Democratic Iowa State Rep. Josh Turek defended missing nearly 58% of legislature votes by citing campaign town halls across all 99 counties.
story: Iowa Senate GOP candidate Ashley Hinson blasted her Democratic opponent, Rep. Josh Turek, for his 42% attendance rate on state votes in the 2026 legislative session during an Oct. 13 debate between the pair. Credit: WHO13

Democratic Iowa State Rep. Josh Turek defended his attendance record after being called out by his opponent, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, during a Tuesday night debate for the state's open Senate seat.
Hinson remarked on Turek's absences while responding to a question posed to both candidates about Iowa's rising cancer rates.

"You have to show up to vote for things like pediatric cancer research, and I've invested in legislation to make sure that we're redirecting those resources to get to where it needs to go to help get to the bottom of this cancer crisis," Hinson said.
As Fox News Digital first uncovered, Turek missed 261 votes in Iowa's state legislature from Jan. 12, 2026, through May 3, representing nearly 58% of the total votes during that time.
The debate's moderator asked Turek directly why he missed the votes.
DEM SENATE HOPEFUL RIPPED AS 'ABSENTEE LEGISLATOR' AFTER MISSING NEARLY 60% OF VOTES

Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson, right, speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Josh Turek at WHO 13, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Charlie Neibergall)
"I have gone out there, and I have met with Iowans all over the state, all 99 counties, hundreds of public forums," Turek responded.
FOX NEWS POLL: TUREK, HINSON IN CLOSE IOWA SENATE RACE

"Meanwhile, Ashley Hinson, since she's decided to run for U.S. Senate, has not done one in-person town forum. Also, in my first three years in the legislature, [I had] more than a 90% attendance record," Turek continued.
"I want to ask again, though, why did you miss those votes?" the moderator repeated.
MEDIA NARRATIVE PREDICTING BLUE WAVE IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE NOT MESHING WITH LOCAL REPUBLICANS: 'FIRED UP'

Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Josh Turek speaks during a televised debate with Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson at WHO 13, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Charlie Neibergall)

"I'm out campaigning. I'm out meeting Iowans all over all 99 counties. I've done hundreds of in-person town halls. Meanwhile, Ashley Hinson, since she's running for the U.S. Senate, has not done a single in-person town hall," he said.
Hinson objected to the notion that she hasn't done any town halls during the campaign cycle.
FOX NEWS POLL: A CLOSE SENATE CONTEST IS BREWING IN IOWA

"I've done more town halls than the percentage of time he showed up to work this year. 42% of the time is all Rep. Turek showed up to work this year. That's two out of every five days of work," Hinson said.

"Iowans, if you're watching tonight, you should know if you don't show up to work two out of five days, you're not getting a promotion. You're getting fired. I am proud of my bipartisan record working with both parties to get things across the finish line. I rank in the top 20% of bipartisan lawmakers in Congress and I have a 99% attendance record even while running a statewide campaign," she concluded.
OBAMA ENDORSES DEMOCRATIC IOWA STATE REP RUNNING FOR US SENATE AGAINST TRUMP-BACKED HOUSE REPUBLICAN

Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Josh Turek at WHO 13, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Charlie Neibergall)
Turek, before the moderator moved on, chimed in, adding, "She also missed 193 votes."

A spokesperson for the Hinson campaign clarified to Fox News Digital that the 193 votes Hinson missed accounted for her entire time in Congress, while the 261 votes Turek missed were in the 2026 legislative session alone.
IOWA GOP GOVERNOR NOMINEE RECOUNTS VIRAL CLASH THAT PUT OBAMA ON THE SPOT AT 2009 TOWN HALL
The Hinson campaign also disputed the idea that she hasn't held any town halls.

"Since being elected to Congress, Ashley Hinson has held 47 in-person town halls and more than 30 telephone town halls — speaking directly to Iowans about the issues that matter most to them," Billy Fuerst, the Hinson campaign communications director, told Fox News Digital.
TRUMP-BACKED IOWA US SENATE HOPEFUL SAYS IRAN WAR MUST 'BE BROUGHT TO A SUCCESSFUL AND IMMEDIATE END'

"Ashley has a 98.8% lifetime voting record while Josh Turek registered a 42% voting record in the State House this year. Ashley missed 16% (94 of 553) of committee amendment votes over the course of her congressional tenure, but has been present for all final passage votes (final passage votes include the amendment language) in her time on the Appropriations Committee — 70 total bills since 2021," Fuerst concluded.
Rep. Turek and his campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital for comment.

title: Jamaica accepts first flight of third-country deportations from US amid looming Supreme Court battle
summary: Jamaica received its first flight of 22 third-country deportees at Kingston's Norman Manley International Airport under a new U.S. agreement.
story: Third-country nationals from the United States arrived in Jamaica Tuesday under a new agreement. (Associated Press)
Jamaica began receiving third-country deportations from the U.S. this week, with the first flight of migrants arriving on Tuesday.
President Donald Trump's administration has used the third-country policy to deport migrants who claim that their home countries are too dangerous to return to.
Tuesday's flight saw 22 migrants land at Kingston’s Norman Manley International Airport in Jamaica.

LIBERIA AGREES TO ACCEPT 1,200 THIRD-COUNTRY DEPORTEES FROM US WITHIN A YEAR

title: Foul-mouthed anti-war protesters repeatedly derail Hegseth's remarks at Army event in DC
summary: Protesters branded Pete Hegseth a "war criminal" and "coward" at his AUSA panel focused on Project Agincourt and autonomous weapons systems.
story: Demonstrators disrupted War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s appearance at the Association of the United States Army’s annual conference in Washington, where senior military leaders gathered to discuss the Pentagon’s plans for autonomous warfare.

Protesters repeatedly interrupted War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s headline appearance at the Army’s biggest annual conference on Wednesday, calling him a "war criminal" and a "coward" in protest of the Iran war.
At least five times in the first half hour of a panel, foul-mouthed anti-war protesters shouted at Hegseth, calling him a "f---ing Nazi" among other insults.

Hegseth responded with chuckles and sarcastic comments, at first — but his reactions became increasingly short and irritated as he slammed the "semi-coordinated" attack as one-by-one protesters emerged among the crowd in Washington, D.C.

A protestor is removed after interrupting a discussion with U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth during the U.S. Army's 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center on October 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Secretary Hegseth participated in a discussion on the future of autonomous warfare. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., on October 14, 2026. The AUSA Meeting and Exposition is a defense trade show and networking event for the global defense community. (Jim WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)
PETE HEGSETH HEADS TO CAPITOL HILL TO DEFEND TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS 60-DAY CONGRESSIONAL DEADLINE LOOMS
"You’re not a warrior you’re a coward!" one demonstrator shouted at Hegseth. "Children in Gaza are starving! He is a war criminal!"
"She thinks highly of me," the Pentagon chief quipped after one outburst, which led to brief applause from the crowd.

The protesters were spread among the room and waited a few minutes between outbursts to interrupt the panel with their anti-war messages. As Hegseth saw a pattern emerging among the outbreaks, he acknowledged: "Appears we have a bit of a tactic."
"The protesters are spouting off slogans, Iran really will never have a nuclear weapon," he later added.
The demonstrators were forcibly removed by security for the event — with at least one woman needing to be carried out of the room by multiple officers while she continued to scream her protest.

A protestor is removed by security personnel as Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., on October 14, 2026. The AUSA Meeting and Exposition is a defense trade show and networking event for the global defense community. (Jim WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)

"The First Amendment right to protest is fundamental. However, everyone who registers to attend the Annual Meeting and enters the convention center does so after agreeing to abide by a code of conduct, so the protestors’ outbursts were certainly not appropriate during today’s forum," the Association of the U.S. Army said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"The acting Army Secretary organized, and we were honored to host, a historic forum to discuss a critical issue that directly affects national security. We’re grateful for the swift action of security and the Metropolitan Police Department to ensure this important discussion could continue."

The panel with Hegseth included acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink and assistant Secretary for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict Derrick Anderson.
As the disruptions continued, the speakers stopped pausing amid the din of shouting and tried to talk over the protesters.

It’s unclear how the protesters received credentials to attend the event known as AUSA, which largely brings together Army brass and the defense contractors that service them. The event set an attendance record of 41,000 people this year.
EMERGING TECH HAS NEW ARMY LEADERS WARNING TROOPS CAN'T ‘AI’ THEIR WAY TO VICTORY ON THE BATTLEFIELD

A protestor is removed by security personnel as Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., on October 14, 2026. The AUSA Meeting and Exposition is a defense trade show and networking event for the global defense community. (Jim WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)
The panel focused on Project Agincourt, the Pentagon’s initiative to accelerate the development and deployment of autonomous weapons and military systems.

title: Man posing as NFL player accused of conning women out of $1.3M
summary: Domonique DuBose spotted red flags when a man on Hinge with 85,000 followers and a blue checkmark claimed to be a San Francisco 49ers player.
story: A man claiming to play for the San Francisco 49ers matched with a woman on a dating app, but Domonique DuBose had her doubts. When DuBose joined The CyberGuy Report podcast, she explained how she became suspicious of a man who allegedly used a fake NFL identity to pursue women and promote fraudulent investments.

A man claiming to play for the San Francisco 49ers matches with you on a dating app. His Instagram has 85,000 followers and a blue checkmark. There are videos showing what appears to be his football lifestyle. He drives luxury cars and seems to have plenty of money. So, would you believe him?

Domonique DuBose had her doubts. When she joined me on The CyberGuy Report podcast, she explained how she became suspicious of a man who allegedly used a fake NFL identity to pursue women and promote fraudulent investments. Federal prosecutors say Daejon Labrayae Love and an alleged accomplice received approximately $1.3 million from at least 26 women.

Love pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a felony charge of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and a public defender representing him did not reply to a request for comment. Magistrate Judge Jolie A. Russo ordered Love detained as a flight risk.

DuBose recognized warning signs and avoided losing any money herself. "Basically, I caught on right away," DuBose told me. What she uncovered raises serious questions about how easily someone can fake an identity online and how you can spot the warning signs before it's too late.

‘TINDER SWINDLER’ ROMANCE FRAUDSTER PROMISES ‘SAFE’ DATING APP – USING INTEL FROM CON MAN PLAYBOOK

According to an FBI affidavit, investigators allege Daejon Love used football-related imagery to support claims that he was a 49ers player, while representatives of the team and NFL said he had never been employed by either organization. (FBI via court documents)
How the fake 49ers player made his story believable

According to DuBose, Love's Instagram account looked like something you might expect from a professional athlete. His posts showed him wearing San Francisco 49ers clothing and enjoying an expensive lifestyle. There were also videos from football-related locations, including footage that appeared connected to the Super Bowl in New Orleans.
"It looked valid. I mean, he had 85,000 followers. He had a blue check," DuBose recalled. She even contacted a friend who had played for the 49ers.

Surprisingly, she says that friend initially supported Love's story. Still, she continued investigating. "I looked at everything from the NFL roster for the Niners to IR to practice squad," she explained.

She also searched his college football history, looking for evidence that he had actually played at the professional level. Another detail bothered her. Nearly every photo seemed to feature 49ers clothing. To DuBose, who knew professional football players, that constant display of team merchandise seemed unusual. Federal investigators later confirmed with representatives of the NFL and the 49ers that Love had never been employed by either organization. That's what makes this case so troubling. A convincing social media profile can make someone seem credible long before anyone checks the facts behind it.
The dating app red flags that caught her attention
DuBose said she met Love on Hinge. His profile described him as an NFL receiver, but their first interactions made her uncomfortable. "It was really fast how he wanted to get my number," she told me.

Instead of sharing her personal number, she took a precaution that limited how much information he could access. "I gave him my work cell phone number instead of my own phone number, and he started texting me."

Then came an unusual flood of attention. Love sent several videos and voice recordings almost immediately. One recording played during our podcast interview included this opening: "So what's up, beautiful? I had to shoot my shot with you." The messages also included extravagant claims about his wealth and how much he wanted to spend time with her. For DuBose, the pace of the attention felt strange. "And it was just so fast. It was so rapid," she recalled.

Some of his other claims raised even more questions. DuBose said he talked about coming from a wealthy Swiss family and having ownership interests involving Gucci stores. She struggled to reconcile those stories with his supposed NFL career. Rather than accepting the explanation, she kept checking.
The many identities behind the alleged $1.3 million scam

Love's supposed football career was only one part of the alleged operation. During our podcast conversation, I asked DuBose about his different identities. She explained that he appeared to have more than two, with different names and professional backgrounds depending on whom he approached. According to federal investigators, Love used several names, including Jon Love, Daejon Love, Avril Lyto Love and Jordan Love. His professional identity also changed depending on the person he approached. "He was a real estate investor. He was a day trader," DuBose explained.

Prosecutors say Love used those claims to convince women that he had access to lucrative investment opportunities. His alleged accomplice, Taylor Jamie Chan, posed as a financial advisor who helped manage Love's fortune, court records allege. Together, they allegedly used fake bank and investment accounts showing enormous balances. They also staged FaceTime calls displaying fabricated investment gains. Some women even took out personal loans after Love promised they would quickly be repaid, the affidavit says.
READ THE AFFIDAVIT – APP USERS, CLICK HERE:

DuBose told me that some women appeared to receive early investment returns, which encouraged them to invest more. However, federal investigators say none of the victims they interviewed reported receiving actual returns after sending money. When women ran out of money or started asking too many questions, prosecutors allege Love cut off contact.
An FBI affidavit details how Daejon Labrayae Love allegedly used a fake 49ers persona, custom helmets and prop money to defraud 26 women of $1.3M. (Getty Images)
More women come forward in the fake NFL player case

The federal investigation has grown since the arrests. On Sept. 18, the FBI reported that 35 additional women had come forward claiming they were defrauded. Investigators were still working to verify those allegations. If confirmed, the number of identified victims would rise from 26 to 61. For DuBose, the emotional damage described by women who say they encountered Love has been particularly painful. She told me that some women described relationships lasting years. Others said they became deeply involved with someone whose identity they never fully understood. "There's some that dated him for 11, 12, 13 years off and on," she said.

Those longer timelines reflect what women reportedly told DuBose. They extend beyond the February 2022 start date of the alleged financial scheme documented by federal investigators. "It breaks my heart," she told me during our interview. She was especially disturbed by the emotional vulnerability that someone could exploit when a person believes a relationship is genuine. "And using that to your advantage is just sick."

DuBose also told me that she would like to confront Love about his alleged actions. After hearing so many stories, there's one answer she still wants. "I want to know why." The FBI has encouraged potential victims to come forward, even if they feel embarrassed about what happened. Investigators say reports from additional people may help them understand the full scope of the alleged scheme.
Can dating apps do more to stop fake identities?

One of the biggest questions raised by this case involves the platforms where these relationships begin. A blue checkmark and a large online following can make an account appear trustworthy. However, verification features vary by platform, and confirming an account holder's identity does not establish that their claimed career or wealth is genuine. DuBose expressed frustration about how easily someone can construct a false life on dating apps. "As far as the dating apps go, you can be whoever you want on those dating apps. And that's the scary part."

She acknowledged that some platforms offer identity checks. However, she questioned whether those checks could ever guarantee that someone was telling the truth about their background. That's a concern worth considering. A person can use their real name and still make false claims about their job. They can also provide authentic photographs while exaggerating their wealth. For anyone meeting a stranger online, independent verification remains an important safeguard.
LUTHER DAVIS ALLEGEDLY WORE DISGUISES TO POSE AS NFL PLAYERS IN MULTI-MILLION DOLLAR LOAN FRAUD SCHEME
How to protect yourself from fake dating profiles
You can still meet people online while taking precautions against fraud. These steps can help you identify suspicious behavior before a relationship becomes financially risky.

If someone says they play professional sports or hold a prestigious position, check official organizational records. Don't rely on social media search results alone. For example, NFL teams publish player rosters that you can check against someone's claims.

Excessive attention early in a conversation may be an attempt to establish trust before introducing a financial request. Pay attention if someone immediately wants to move off the dating app or begins discussing a serious relationship before you've had time to get acquainted.
There are precautions you can take against fraud when meeting someone on a dating app. (Alicia Windzio/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Communicate through the dating app until you feel comfortable. A separate phone number can help limit exposure, although it won't eliminate every risk. Avoid sharing your home address or workplace details with someone you have only recently met online.

Look for inconsistent names or multiple profiles using the same images. A reverse image search may reveal whether someone has copied photographs from another person's account. Our CyberGuy article explains how to avoid dating app scammers.

Be especially skeptical of guaranteed returns or requests to take out personal loans. Independently check any financial opportunity before considering it. Someone who genuinely cares about you should respect your decision to keep your finances separate.

Conflicting information about someone's background deserves a closer look. Give yourself time to verify details without pressure. If the person becomes defensive or tries to discourage you from checking their claims, consider that another warning sign. DuBose continues taking precautions when meeting new people. She told me that she checks phone numbers and tries to establish whether someone is using a legitimate identity. "If you text me the moment you text me, I'm reverse checking your number. I'm making sure your name is valid." A reverse lookup can provide useful clues, although scammers may use spoofed numbers or accounts registered under other people's names.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
What to do if you already sent money to a scammer
If you suspect someone has deceived you through a dating app, act quickly. Your chances of recovering money may depend on how you paid and how soon you report the transaction.

Explain what happened and ask whether it can reverse or recall the payment. If you sent money through a wire transfer or payment app, contact that service's fraud department as soon as possible. Speed can be important when attempting to recover funds.

Save screenshots of messages and dating profiles. Keep financial transaction records that could help investigators. Don't delete conversations before documenting them, even if the experience is upsetting.

An Instagram account associated with Daejon Love displayed San Francisco 49ers gear and luxury vehicles, helping support his alleged false identity as an NFL player. (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon)

File a complaint through IC3.gov and provide as much information as possible. Include the person's usernames, phone numbers and payment details. You can also report suspected fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Report the suspicious account so the platform can investigate and take appropriate action. Include any evidence showing that the person misrepresented their identity or requested money.

Criminals sometimes contact fraud victims again, claiming they can retrieve stolen money in exchange for an upfront payment. Be skeptical of anyone promising guaranteed recovery, especially if they request additional payments or sensitive financial information. If you have information involving Daejon Love or Taylor Chan specifically, the FBI requests tips through tips.fbi.gov or 1-800-CALL-FBI.
Kurt's key takeaways

What stayed with me after speaking with Domonique DuBose on The CyberGuy Report podcast was how convincing this alleged deception became. We're talking about someone who reportedly built an entire lifestyle around a career he never had. He used the credibility of a major NFL team and social media to get people to believe him. Some allegedly trusted him with significant amounts of money. During our conversation, I raised a question that I think deserves a serious answer. These social media companies can collect an extraordinary amount of information about us. As I put it on the podcast, "these social media companies know what toothbrush we're using and when we're going to buy a loaf of bread." So why does it remain so difficult to identify someone who builds a false professional identity and uses it to target people? I also admire how thoroughly DuBose investigated the situation. Even when someone she knew appeared to validate the story, she continued asking questions. Her experience is a reminder that you should never feel pressured to trust someone simply because their online life looks convincing.

If a dating app verifies someone's identity but that person turns out to be lying about who they are, should the platform share responsibility for the damage? Or do you believe people should be entirely responsible for protecting themselves? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Your phone may reveal doctor, church and pharmacy visits
summary: Your phone's location data can expose visits to doctors, pharmacies and places of worship. The FTC took action against data brokers selling this data.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson lays out how to limit what health apps used by insurance companies can track about you, the user.

Nobody needs to follow you to know where you went this week. The phone in your pocket can already keep a record of your movements. And parts of that information can end up in the hands of other companies.

Your pharmacy. Your cardiologist. The church you attend on Sunday morning. The support group you'd rather nobody knew about. None of it necessarily comes from hacking. It can come from ordinary apps you installed yourself and the permissions you gave them. Here's how your movements can get out, who buys location data and the settings that can limit how much gets shared.
Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.
See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com.
WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE
A smartphone can share location and other device data that may reveal sensitive details about where you go. (Tero Vesalainen/Getty Images)
Your phone can carry an advertising identifier

Smartphones can use advertising identifiers that help advertisers and developers measure ads and activity. On Apple devices, the system advertising identifier is known as the IDFA. Android devices can use Google's advertising ID.

Advertising identifiers can help connect activity across apps when apps and advertising systems are permitted to use them. Combined with location data and other signals, those identifiers can help companies build a much more detailed trail of where a device has been.

And a trail stops being anonymous fast. A device that sleeps at your address every night and turns up at a dialysis center every Tuesday and Thursday isn't much of a mystery to anyone who can connect those locations with other identifying information.
The apps hand it off, and it keeps moving

An app asks for your location. Often for a fair reason, like providing a local forecast or showing the nearest pharmacy. What many people don't realize is that apps can include advertising and analytics software from outside companies. Depending on the app, its permissions and its privacy practices, that technology may collect or receive information about your device and location. Location information can also become part of the digital advertising ecosystem, where information about a device can pass among multiple companies. Once location data leaves your phone, controlling where it goes next becomes much harder.
Federal regulators have already gone after this

This isn't a theory about what could happen. The government spent years fighting one such case in court. On May 4, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission announced a settlement that bars the data broker Kochava and its subsidiary, Collective Data Solutions, from selling, sharing or disclosing sensitive location data without people's affirmative express consent, subject to the terms of the order. The FTC alleged Kochava sold location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices that could track people to health facilities, places of worship and other sensitive locations. Kochava did not admit wrongdoing. Kochava wasn't alone. In December 2024, the FTC took action against two more location data companies, Gravy Analytics and Mobilewalla, over allegations involving the sale of sensitive location data.
Then one of them got robbed

In January 2025, Gravy Analytics was breached. A hacker posted what they claimed was 17 terabytes of stolen data on a Russian cybercrime forum. Security researchers examining a sample found more than 30 million location points, including phones at the White House, the Kremlin and military bases around the world. The data reportedly came from everyday apps, including games and dating apps. Think about what that means. A company collects movements. Regulators take action over how sensitive location data gets handled. Then criminals allegedly obtain a massive collection of data anyway.
What your movements actually tell a stranger
Strip out the technical language. A few weeks of location data can potentially reveal:

Which clinic you go to and how often you go backWhich house of worship you attend and whether you still doWhether anyone else appears to live at your addressWhat hours your home may sit emptyWhich relatives you visit and on what day
Which clinic you go to and how often you go back
Which house of worship you attend and whether you still do
Whether anyone else appears to live at your address
What hours your home may sit empty
Which relatives you visit and on what day

Those last few can turn a privacy problem into a safety concern. A device that regularly leaves a home at the same time and returns two hours later can reveal patterns about when someone may be away. Location information can also make a scam call more convincing. "I'm calling from the billing office at the clinic on Oak Street about your visit last week" is much harder to dismiss when the clinic and timing happen to be correct. And with Medicare Open Enrollment beginning October 15, a caller who seems to know your doctor or pharmacy may sound more convincing than a random scammer.
'But I never share my location'

If you've ever tapped "Allow" on a weather app, a store app or a game, you may have shared it. You might have granted that permission years ago and forgotten about it. Even apps without precise location permission may be able to estimate your general area through information such as your internet connection. You can't make yourself invisible, but you can make your movements harder to track.
What you can do about it

You can't stop your phone from knowing where you are and still use every location-based feature. But you can limit which apps get that information and reduce some of the identifiers used for advertising and tracking. None of this takes technical skill, and you can tackle one part at a time.
Start here: limit advertising tracking
Advertising identifiers aren't the only way companies can recognize a device, but limiting them can remove one tool used to connect activity for advertising purposes.
First, control whether apps can request permission to track you across other companies' apps and websites:
Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap TrackingTurn off Allow Apps to Request to Track
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Tracking
Turn off Allow Apps to Request to Track
When this setting is off, apps that request permission to track are treated as though you selected Ask App Not to Track. They cannot access Apple's system advertising identifier, known as the IDFA.
Apple also has a separate setting for ads that Apple itself delivers:
Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap Apple AdvertisingTurn off Personalized Ads
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Apple Advertising
Turn off Personalized Ads
This second setting limits how Apple personalizes the ads it delivers in services such as the App Store, Apple News and Stocks. It is separate from the app-tracking control above.
THE SCAMMER AT YOUR DOCTOR'S OFFICE MAY ALREADY KNOW WHO YOU ARE
Social media apps collect more data than many users realize, from clicks and contacts to location history. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
To check your advertising ID controls:
Open SettingsTap Security and privacyScroll down and tap More privacy settingsOpen AdsTap Delete advertising ID if that option appearsConfirm your choice
Open Settings
Tap Security and privacy
Scroll down and tap More privacy settings
Open Ads
Tap Delete advertising ID if that option appears
Confirm your choice
Depending on your Galaxy model and software configuration, you may also find Google's advertising controls through Settings > Google > All services > Ads.
Deleting the advertising ID prevents apps from accessing that particular Google advertising identifier. It does not prevent every form of advertising, analytics or device identification.
Open SettingsTap Security & PrivacyTap Privacy controlsTap AdsTap Delete advertising IDConfirm your choice
Open Settings
Tap Security & Privacy
Tap Privacy controls
Tap Ads
Tap Delete advertising ID
Confirm your choice

Google says deleting the advertising ID removes that identifier. Apps that try to access it receive a string of zeros instead. Apps can still have their own privacy and advertising settings, so this does not eliminate every form of tracking.
Next: tighten location permissions
Now look at which apps can see where you are and whether they really need that access.

Open SettingsTap Privacy & SecurityTap Location ServicesScroll through the list of appsTap an app you want to reviewChoose the appropriate access, such as Never, Ask Next Time or When I Share or While Using the AppIf the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Precise Location
Open Settings
Tap Privacy & Security
Tap Location Services
Scroll through the list of apps
Tap an app you want to review
Choose the appropriate access, such as Never, Ask Next Time or When I Share or While Using the App
If the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Precise Location
You don't have to turn Location Services off completely. Doing so can interfere with useful features. Instead, focus on apps that have more access than they need.

Open SettingsTap LocationTap App permissions or App location permissionsReview the apps that can access your locationTap an app you want to changeSelect the appropriate option, such as Don't allow, Ask every time or Allow only while using the appIf the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Use precise location
Open Settings
Tap Location
Tap App permissions or App location permissions
Review the apps that can access your location
Tap an app you want to change
Select the appropriate option, such as Don't allow, Ask every time or Allow only while using the app
If the app doesn't need your exact location, turn off Use precise location
Pay particular attention to apps allowed to access your location all the time. Weather, shopping and similar apps often don't need continuous background access.
YOUR HOME IS EMPTY. DO BURGLARS ALREADY KNOW?
Data broker listings often include sensitive details like your address, phone number and relatives, making removal a critical first step. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Open SettingsTap LocationTap App location permissionsReview the apps under categories such as Allowed all the time, Allowed only while in use, Ask every time or allow when I share and Not allowedTap an app you want to changeChoose the level of location access it actually needsTurn off Use precise location when an approximate location is enough
Open Settings
Tap Location
Tap App location permissions
Review the apps under categories such as Allowed all the time, Allowed only while in use, Ask every time or allow when I share and Not allowed
Tap an app you want to change
Choose the level of location access it actually needs
Turn off Use precise location when an approximate location is enough
A weather app, for example, usually doesn't need to know exactly where you're standing. Navigation is one situation where precise location makes much more sense.
Then: clear out what you're not using

Delete dormant apps. Every unused app is another set of permissions and data practices you may have forgotten about. If you haven't opened an app since last year and no longer need it, consider deleting it.
Finally: do it for your parents too

If you have older relatives, their phones are worth checking next. They may be carrying years of old app permissions, and scammers frequently target older adults. Sit down with them for 10 minutes the next time you visit. Review location permissions, advertising controls and apps they no longer use.
The half your phone settings can't reach

Changing these settings can reduce future collection and sharing, but it doesn't erase information that companies may have already collected. And here's the piece many people miss. A location trail by itself may consist largely of coordinates and device information. It becomes much more revealing when someone can connect those movements with a name, home address, phone number or relatives. Some of that identifying information can come from people-search and data broker sites that publish or sell personal details. You can run a quick free scan to see what a scammer would see if they looked you up right now. If it shows details you never agreed to publish, you'll be able to take action and get them removed.

This is where I strongly recommend using a personal data removal service. These services can automatically send removal requests to hundreds of data brokers, including people-search websites, on your behalf. They can also keep monitoring and resubmitting requests when your information reappears, which is important because data can return even after it has been removed. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

Your phone can reveal far more about your life than you may realize. Location data can expose visits to doctors, pharmacies, places of worship and other sensitive locations, especially when it gets combined with advertising identifiers and other information about you. The FTC's actions against location data brokers show this is not a hypothetical privacy problem. And the Gravy Analytics breach showed what can happen when enormous collections of location information fall into the wrong hands. I would start by reviewing which apps have access to your location and removing access from anything that doesn't truly need it. Then limit app tracking on your iPhone or delete your advertising ID on Android if that option is available. These changes won't make you invisible, but they can reduce the amount of information available to build a detailed trail of where you go. And don't forget the phones belonging to parents or older relatives. Years of forgotten app permissions can leave far more information exposed than they realize.

title: French supermarkets face millions in losses after cyberattack hits refrigerators nationwide
summary: Hackers targeted Danfoss refrigerator controls across French supermarkets, forcing chains like Carrefour and Monoprix to discard massive food stocks.
story: A sophisticated cyberattack targets hundreds of French supermarkets by hacking refrigerators to heat up to 122°F. Ashley Webster reports how the temperature spike spoiled massive amounts of food and sparked fires across Europe.

A cyberattack in France forced multiple grocery stores to discard large amounts of temperature-sensitive product after hackers turned the heat up on food refrigerators in hundreds of stores across at least five chain brands.
The hack, according to Reuters and European officials, affected chains such as Carrefour, Monoprix, Les Mousquetaires, E. Leclerc and Coopérative U.
The CEO of Coopérative U, a retail group structured as a cooperative of independently owned businesses, confirmed the cyberattack in a Monday post on X.
"I confirm that a cyberattack has been affecting, since last night, the cold production facilities of several stores in our network Coopérative U," he wrote in the post.
FOREIGN HACKERS BREACH TWO MORE US WATER UTILITIES, THREATEN SAFETY OF COLORADO RESIDENTS

View of the closed frozen food aisle at a supermarket near Nantes after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores, France, October 12, 2026. (REUTERS/Stephane Mahe)

"Our teams are fully mobilized, in coordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible. An investigation will be necessary to shed full light on this attack. Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable," he concluded.
IF HACKERS CRIPPLE AMERICA'S WATER, THE CONSEQUENCES COULD BE CATASTROPHIC
The Paris prosecutor's office also confirmed the cyberattack, characterizing it as a "large-scale" attack that affected "connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France."
Carrefour said roughly 80 of its stores were affected while Monoprix, which operates 490 stores in France according to Reuters, said 5% of its stores were affected.

View of the closed frozen food aisle at a supermarket near Nantes after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores, France, October 12, 2026. (REUTERS/Stephane Mahe)
IRAN-LINKED HACKERS SUSPECTED IN UK POWER-PLANT SHUTDOWN AFTER ALLEGED MINNESOTA WATER ATTACK

Les Mousquetaires said fridges at approximately 150 of its stores were heated up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) for six hours. A company spokesperson also said all affected food had been discarded, according to Reuters.
While the incident's financial toll on the supermarket has yet to be officially tabulated, experts estimated the losses to be upwards of 10 million euros, equivalent to roughly $11.2 million.
INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT
The attack likely resulted in the loss of "tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day," Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard said during a televised interview in France, according to Reuters.
A source with knowledge of the refrigerator systems reportedly told AFP that the hackers targeted refrigerator controls systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES

Danfoss, in turn, told AFP that most of the affected equipment were "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates." The company also added that some of the systems affected were using "outdated firmware" which it had long-counseled its purchasers to update.
Danfoss did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu arrives to deliver a statement at the Hotel Matignon in Paris, Monday, Oct. 6, 2025. (Ludovic Marin, Pool)
TRUMP PLAN TAPS US FIRMS TO FIGHT FOREIGN CYBERCRIME

French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has instructed France's National Cyber security Agency (ANSSI) to conduct an investigation. ANSSI has already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor," a source close to Lecornu reportedly told AFP.
Christophe Hansen, the European Union's Commissioner for Agriculture and Food, denounced the attack as an affront on European food safety.
IRANIAN HACKERS ATTACKED OUR WATER SYSTEMS. HERE ARE 5 THINGS OUR LEADERS NEED TO DO NOW

"I strongly condemn the cyberattack targeting food products at Intermarche, Cooperative U, Leclerc. Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponization of food has become a reality," he said in a Monday post on X.

title: Stop losing photo quality when you share pictures
summary: iOS 27 finally lets iPhone Shared Albums store photos and videos at full resolution in iCloud, but new items count toward the owner's storage.
story: Apple's newly unveiled foldable iPhone Duo sparks significant consumer interest despite a hefty $1,999 starting price tag. On 'Varney & Co.', Taylor Riggs explains the premium device's unique dual-screen capability and ultra-thin design. Host Stuart Varney admits he plans to purchase the high-end smartphone, which can cost up to $3,000 for the two-terabyte storage model.

You take a great photo, send it to someone and then hear the question nobody wants to hear: "Why does this look blurry?" That can happen because some sharing methods resize or compress photos before they reach the other person. The image may still look fine on a phone screen, but zoom in or try to print it and the lost detail becomes easier to spot.

With iOS 27, Apple is addressing one long-standing version of that problem. Shared Albums can now store newly added photos and videos in their original formats at full resolution. Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel phones also have built-in ways to send photo files without relying on a messaging app that may shrink them along the way.
