title: Inside the protest playbook to vilify Israel on 'global day of action'
summary: Global Alliance for Palestine distributed a detailed playbook urging groups to shut down city squares and blockade corporate hubs across continents.
story: Fox News host Greg Gutfeld and the panel discuss anti-Israel protests as the nation remembers the October 7 terrorist attack.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — As demonstrators, including the headline-grabbing CodePink agitators, descend on the nation's capital late Saturday afternoon for a "coordinated global day of action" against Israel, they will join a worldwide wave of marches and planned disruptions that may appear to be unfolding independently.

In Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on Friday, anti-Israel demonstrators carried signs deploying emotionally charged language against Israel, including one featuring a Palestinian flag and a bloodied hand with the message, "STOP GENOCIDE."
Nearby, two women carrying mock machine guns flanked a cardboard image of a handcuffed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with a noose around his neck.

Anti-Israel demonstrators carry a cutout depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alongside mock cardboard weapons and placards during a rally Oct. 9, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.  (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)

But a Fox News Digital investigation has found that, long before the first demonstrators gathered, the messages for the protest's "communications framing" and transnational action plan had already been written, the banners designed, the tactics circulated and the media strategy laid out to "turn public outrage into collective leverage."
LAWMAKERS THROW OUT 'TROJAN HORSE' ACTIVISTS THEY SAY ARE ENGAGED IN AMERICAN SUBVERSION

The campaign documents reveal that coalition organizers instructed participating groups to direct protesters to "shut down city squares," "encircle government buildings" and "blockade complicit corporate hubs."
The document declares, "This is not a symbolic march and not a routine protest."
Fox News Digital identified 179 organizations in the coalition, while an interactive Google Map published by the network lists 322 events scheduled across three days through Sunday.

They include a rally on an "Intifada Trail" in Saint John, New Brunswick, Canada; a protest in Bangladesh by the "Bangladesh Intifada Youth Collection"; and actions in South Africa by "Social Intifada."
All three use "intifada," a term associated with Palestinian uprisings against Israel, including periods marked by deadly terrorist attacks. Activists describe the term as a call for resistance.

The global coordination illustrates how contemporary protest movements combine international leadership, local activist networks, standardized visual branding, emotionally charged messaging and traditional news outreach into a single mobilization infrastructure in which professional political organizing amplifies the sincerely held convictions of individual demonstrators.
Organizers from Global Action for Palestine shared a map for Global Day of Action events for 2026. (Global Alliance for Palestine)

Among the participating organizations is CodePink, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that has received $1.33 million from Neville Roy Singham, a Shanghai-based tech tycoon who has funneled $278 million into a network of nonprofits under scrutiny by the House Ways and Means Committee and its chairman, Rep. Jason Smith, over allegations that some operate as "Trojan horses" and proxies for the Chinese Communist Party and other malign foreign interests. CodePink and other organizations under scrutiny have denied wrongdoing.

Two days ago, CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin and D.C. coordinator Olivia DiNucci dispatched a letter to members, directing them to join the "Feminist Contingent" at the Library of Congress for the "global day of action."
"And don't forget to WEAR PINK!" they noted.

The network's connections were also visible last week, when CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans, who married Singham in 2017, joined an anti-Israel protest in New York City, marching behind a band of activists from Revolutionary Communists of America as they chanted, "Long live the intifada."
Evans told Fox News Digital Singham supports CodePink's efforts and the "amazing work" nonprofits are doing to "stand up when violent things are happening."

Taken together, the documents reveal a coordinated protest and influence campaign spanning continents, combining accusations of Israeli "genocide," attacks on the news media, workplace and university walkouts, blockades, political lobbying and carefully orchestrated publicity.

A review of the planning documents for the global protests reveals the machinery behind the wave of anti-Israel demonstrations across continents as not only a protest campaign but a psychological operation.

In a document, leaders of the Global Alliance for Palestine"spell out "What Organisations Can Do" to oppose the state of Israel and support a "global day of action" Oct. 7, 2026. (Global Alliance for Palestine)

At the center of the international mobilization are three organizations identified in the campaign documents: the Global Alliance for the Palestinian Territories, launched in July 2025 in London as a "truly international popular front for Palestinian liberation"; the Anti-Apartheid Movement for Palestine; and the Global Coalition to End the Occupation of Palestine.
An online directory displays 179 organizational logos from participating groups worldwide. Fox News Digital extracted the names from the logos and built a database of the coalition.
The same pattern of coordinated organizing has emerged in another international protest movement — the "student protests" rolling through France.

A separate Fox News Digital investigation identified a network of 50 organizations coordinating and amplifying those demonstrations. Only 15 were classified as youth- or student-led groups, while the remaining 35 included communist organizations, labor groups, political organizations and professional protest coordinators.
Organizers supplied participating groups with campaign materials, coordination and strategic support to "turn public outrage into collective leverage."

In an August "Launch Statement," the alliance laid out a strategy to synchronize student demonstrations, workplace actions, rallies and civil disobedience across Asia, the Americas, Europe, Africa and the Middle East.

The stated objective wasn't simply to organize demonstrations but to add Israel's war in Gaza to the international media agenda, turning separate protests into a coordinated communications effort intended to shape what audiences around the world see, hear and think about the conflict.
Anti-Israel demonstrators hold a Palestinian flag and signage during a rally Oct. 9, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, as part of a "global day of action" against Israel.  (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)
But the most revealing aspect of the operation may be its stated objective of shaping what the world sees, hears and thinks about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
In a "Launch Statement" in August, the alliance declared that the demonstrations are intended to return Israel's military campaign against Palestinians to the international media agenda.

The campaign materials describe a strategy of synchronizing protests across continents, connecting student demonstrations, workplace actions, rallies and civil disobedience from Asia to the Americas, Europe, Africa and the Middle East.
The result is a coordinated communications campaign designed to transform demonstrations organized by separate groups into the political impact of a single international mobilization.
ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS

Weeks before the demonstrations, the alliance had already prepared a collection of campaign posters in seven languages — English, Arabic, Turkish, Finnish, French, Portuguese and Spanish. They supplied graphics for a large street banner carrying carefully selected slogans, along with protest-sign designs from folders marked "HANDHELD PLACARDS" and "STREET DEMANDS."
One of the downloadable images is a poster with the message "GAZA GENOCIDE" next to graphics of barbed wire and watermelon, both symbols of Palestinian "resistance" against Israel.

In Malaysia, a woman wearing a black-and-white Palestinian keffiyeh raised her fist while holding a printed version of the watermelon and barbed-wire placard, with the organizers' branding in smaller letters on her sign: "GLOBAL ALLIANCE FOR PALESTINE."
Behind her, other women carried the same sign and other signs featuring additional graphics from the same campaign materials.

A woman covers her hairs with a Palestinian keffiyeh scarf and raises her fist while holding a placard reading "Gaza Genocide" during an anti-Israel rally Oct. 9, 2026, in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. The sign is part of a series of downloadable pre-made graphics created by organizers of the global protest. (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)
Other placards held by protesters in Malaysia yesterday read, "HUMANITY IS NOT A CRIME" and "STOP THE GENOCIDE WAR!"
Another downloadable sign, carried in Malaysia, reads: "LET GAZA LIVE!"

The campaign's "Communications Framing" employs familiar techniques of political persuasion: repetition, emotional imagery, collective identity, moral urgency and the portrayal of inaction as complicity.
The materials offer a window into the battle for public attention that increasingly accompanies international conflicts.

Women at an anti-Israel rally on Oct. 9, 2026, in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, hold placards with messages created by the leaders of the Global Alliance for Palestine for protests around the country. The messages read "Humanity Is Not a Crime," "Let Gaza Live" and "Stop the Genocide War." (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)
One poster declares, "You cannot erase a homeland."
Another commands, "End the genocide. Defend the land."
A third combines an image of a child with the message, "Defend the land. Protect its children."
Another repeats the words "Silence normalises" across the background before presenting the word "genocide" in oversized red lettering.

But the campaign's internal messaging guidance goes further, prescribing accusations against Israel and the news media in a section called "Slogans & Hashtags," with "Call to Action & Core Street Demands."
In a "concept paper" for the Global Alliance for Palestine, organizers share guidelines for "Slogans & Hashtags" that carry explicit negative messages about Israel. (Global Alliance for Palestine)
Among its recommended slogans is the blunt declaration: "Israel Kills. The Media Justifies."
Another declares, "1,100 Days of Israeli Genocide — The Killing Continues."
Yet another calls for action under the message, "1,100 Days — From Every Street, One Demand: End Genocide, End Occupation."
Together, the slogans strategically combine accusations of "genocide" with demands for political action, while claiming the media "justifies" Israel's conduct.

In a "concept paper" for the Global Alliance for Palestine, organizers share guidelines for "Communications Framing," including "Core Messages" that intentionally describe Israel negatively. (Global Alliance for Palestine)
In its "Concept Paper," the alliance describes Israel's actions as a "war of extermination" and calls for countries to stop providing weapons to the Israeli state.
The same document instructs participating organizations in its "Communications Framing" to use language that is "disciplined, credible, urgent and impossible to ignore."
It also directs organizers to portray "institutional silence" as part of the problem and public mobilization as necessary to confront what the alliance calls continuing complicity.
The objective isn't simply to communicate a political position but to encourage audiences to emotionally identify with a movement and participate in its activities.
The campaign presents its allegations of "genocide" and other violations of international law as established claims.

On Friday, South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay received the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her work, which included arguing that Israel has committed a "genocide" against Palestinians. Israel disputes the "genocide" accusation.
ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'
The organizing documents go beyond encouraging supporters to attend demonstrations.

Instead, organizers describe a campaign intended to "interrupt business-as-usual" and organize "high-visibility rallies, marches, picket lines, sit-ins and peaceful blockades" at "civic sites, government offices, financial hubs and corporate locations" that its organizers have "identified as complicit in sustaining or normalising Israeli violence."

They also recommend synchronized "workplace, campus and creative interruptions," including "silent walkouts," banner drops, nighttime projections, street theater, "die-ins" and "other highly visible public actions that interrupt normal routines and make the political demand impossible to ignore."
A detailed logistical plan urges organizations to "allocate funds," arrange transportation and establish "legal, stewarding, and participant support."
ISRAELI PM NETANYAHU ARGUES PUBLIC OPINION SHIFT ON ISRAEL 'CORRELATES ALMOST 100%' TO SOCIAL MEDIA

Yahya Sinwar, center, Hamas leader in Gaza; Mahmoud al-Zahar, right, senior Hamas leader; and Mustafa Barghouti, left, secretary general of the National Initiative and supporters of the Palestinian Hamas movement gather during a rally in solidarity with al-Aqsa mosque Oct. 1, 2022 in Gaza City, Gaza.  (Mohammed Dahman/Getty Image)

The campaign's organizational structure brings together prominent political figures with longstanding backgrounds in international politics and anti-Israel activism in Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

A press release for the protests identifies seven members of the international steering committee, including former British Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn, who joined a coalition supporting the Communist Party of Cuba; pro-communist former Greek Finance Minister Yanis Varoufakis; former Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams; Palestinian political leader Mustafa Barghouti; former South African government minister Ronnie Kasrils; Indian activist Varsha Gandikota-Nellutla; and Italian politician Angelo Bonelli.
Anas Altikriti serves as secretary-general.
Jessica Breakey, the campaign's public relations officer, didn't respond to a request for comment.
Beyond the streets, the alliance's strategy documents lay out a plan to convert the demonstrations' visibility into "sustained political pressure" on lawmakers and government institutions.

In a separate advocacy document, organizers urge participating groups to mobilize protesters to write lawmakers, submit coordinated institutional letters and arrange meetings with elected representatives.
The campaign calls for "immediate, total arms embargoes" and "comprehensive state sanctions" against Israel for alleged violations of international law.
It also urges governments to suspend preferential trade agreements and institutional partnerships associated with Israeli policies.

The alliance demands an end to what it calls Israel's "genocide and occupation," without specifying whether its reference to occupation encompasses Gaza, the West Bank or the entire State of Israel. The distinction takes on particular significance amid chants of "from the river to the sea" at anti-Israel demonstrations.

Organizers encourage participating groups to use "targeted, template-driven letters" and "digital briefing toolkits" to support "localised political campaigning," adapting them to their national political systems.

The documents provide direct instructions that participating organizations issue local press releases, distribute "ready-made social-media toolkits," share "graphics across digital channels" and hold briefing sessions to "ensure clear, aligned messaging ahead of the weekend."

Asra Nomani is senior editor of investigations at Fox News Digital. She is a former reporter at the Wall Street Journal, where she covered stories related to money, politics and society. She is the author of "Woke Army: The Red-Green Alliance That Is Undermining America’s Freedom." She can be reached at asra.nomani@fox.com and on X at @asranomani.

title: France is devouring itself as school riots reveal a crisis far bigger than broken classrooms
summary: Student protests in France over crumbling schools expose deep tensions as Jean-Luc Mélenchon's La France Insoumise allegedly exploits the growing unrest.
story: FDD Special Envoy Simone Rodan-Benzaquen says legitimate student grievances have been hijacked by political movements seeking to fuel unrest and deepen divisions across France.

Student protests over crumbling schools despite billions in public spending are fueling a broader crisis in France, and experts warn that the country's mounting financial troubles, President Emmanuel Macron's weakened political center and radical movements are pushing the unrest far beyond its original educational grievances.

Simone Rodan-Benzaquen, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies' senior envoy for Europe, told Fox News Digital in an interview from Paris that what began in September with legitimate complaints about school conditions has increasingly been exploited by political forces seeking confrontation with the state.
"Overall, I'd say the anger is real, but the violence, I would say, is organized," she said, adding that destroying schools would do nothing to improve the education system.
FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION
A protesting student feeds a burnt barrier during a blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris on Oct. 1, 2026. (Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images)

Seventy-two percent of education expenditures went toward salaries, social contributions and pensions for teaching and non-teaching personnel, while just 8.5% went toward investment, including infrastructure and equipment. The figures cover the entire education system, not just high schools, according to France's Education Ministry's 2026 statistical overview.

Harvey Feigenbaum, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University and an expert on French politics, told Fox News Digital that France's underlying problem is a government caught between expensive social commitments, sluggish economic growth and mounting pressure to cut spending.
"France is in deep debt. It wants to cut its expenses," Feigenbaum said, explaining that years of financial pressure and neglected school facilities have fueled frustration among students.

The scale of the financial predicament is striking. According to Eurostat, French public debt stood at 117.6% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, the third-highest ratio in the European Union, behind Greece and Italy.

Reuters reported Oct. 8 that rising borrowing costs and investor concerns have severely limited the government's ability to resolve unrest through additional spending, a strategy employed during previous waves of French protests.
The financial squeeze has collided with an increasingly fragmented political system, creating opportunities for parties at both ends of the political spectrum to capitalize on public dissatisfaction.
FRENCH SCHOOL RIOTS DEEPEN AS EXPERTS POINT TO FAR-LEFT ALLIANCE FUELING ‘BROADER CONFRONTATION’

Protestors gather around the Monument à la République in Place de la République in Paris on Oct. 4, 2026, during nationwide demonstrations against an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system.  (Veronique de Viguerie/Getty Images)
Macron's political center collapses
For Feigenbaum, the long-term roots of the crisis lie in Macron's political legacy.
When Macron won the presidency in 2017, he promised to move beyond France's traditional left-right divide, combining policies from both sides into a new centrist political movement.
But Feigenbaum argues that the strategy produced an unintended consequence, weakening France's established moderate parties without creating a durable governing coalition to replace them.
"What he ended up doing was attracting the moderate voters from the parties of the moderate left and the parties from the moderate right, and essentially destroyed those parties," Feigenbaum said.
He argued that the collapse of the traditional political center helped create space for more ideologically polarized movements.
"Macron is a smart man, but he's a terrible politician," the professor added.

Macron's controversial pension reforms illustrate the difficulty of persuading French voters to accept reductions in longstanding public benefits, Feigenbaum argued. Those efforts triggered widespread protests, while implementation of the 2023 retirement changes has since been suspended until 2028.
The situation became especially difficult after Macron called snap parliamentary elections in 2024, producing a deeply divided National Assembly without a governing majority.
"Even if the government wanted to do something coherent, they simply don't have the votes to do it," Feigenbaum said.
That paralysis has left Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu handling the immediate unrest while Macron faces questions about the stability of the political system he helped reshape.
FRENCH PM REJECTS POLICE BRUTALITY CLAIMS AFTER TEENS SEVERELY INJURED IN PROTESTS: 'ACCIDENTS HAPPEN'

Protesters hold a Palestinian flag Oct. 6, 2026, the day French high school and university students attend a demonstration in Strasbourg as part of a nationwide day of protests and blockades, voicing anger over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated school buildings, which students blame on years of underinvestment. (Reuters/Kai Pfaffenbach)
Why are France's schools struggling despite billions in spending?
The protests began in the Paris suburbs in September amid complaints about overcrowded classrooms, inadequate heating and cooling, aging buildings and teachers who were not replaced when absent.
Rodan-Benzaquen said the anger reflected years of educational instability, frequent ministerial changes and reforms that have failed to resolve persistent school problems.
She also pointed to a broader sense of anxiety among young people about their economic future, artificial intelligence, climate change and international conflicts.

According to the OECD's September 2026 Education at a Glance report, France spent $16,674 in funding per student in general upper secondary education in 2023, compared with an OECD average of $12,421, adjusted for purchasing power.

Anti-riot police officers face protesting students carrying out blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris Oct. 1, 2026. (Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images)
Yet teachers and students continue to complain about basic shortages.
Responsibility for public high school buildings and equipment falls to regional authorities, while the national government oversees much of the education system, including teacher staffing.
Feigenbaum said France's centralized education structure makes national leaders the focus of public anger when schools fail to deliver.
The pressure has already forced a concession.
Reuters reported Friday that Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced an emergency plan to deploy 3,000 qualified educators to particularly affected schools, costing several dozen million euros.
Student unions welcomed the measure as an initial victory but pledged to continue demonstrating.

The spending figures raise broader questions about whether France's financial and political priorities have left sufficient resources for maintaining school infrastructure and meeting students' needs. They do not, however, establish that teachers' unions or other organized constituencies have improperly diverted funding.
TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the French left-wing La France Insoumise party, delivers a speech during an electoral campaign meeting of the local LFI candidate for French municipal elections in Marseille, southern France, March 7, 2026. (Miguel Medina/AFP via Getty Images)
How the far left entered the unrest
As the demonstrations expanded, the involvement of France's hard-left La France Insoumise party, known as LFI, led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, became an increasingly contentious issue.

Reuters reported Oct. 1 that French intelligence agencies had told a government crisis meeting that LFI and affiliated activists played a role in fomenting the unrest. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez also cited agitators moving between schools to encourage violence.
LFI has denied responsibility and accused authorities of aggravating tensions through their response.
Rodan-Benzaquen said far-left movements were capitalizing on students' frustration.
"There is an obvious instrumentalization, obvious manipulation," she said, arguing that activists were seeking to push some protesters toward violence.
She linked the unrest to what she described as Mélenchon's broader political strategy ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.

"His idea is that, on the one hand, he will scare voters on the right and on the far right, who will then go to vote for the far right, and, on the other hand, he would mobilize his own camp," she said.

Rodan-Benzaquen argued that intensifying political confrontation could help Mélenchon consolidate his support among younger voters and immigrant communities, while portraying the far right as an increasingly serious threat.
She described it as a calculated political strategy rather than a spontaneous response to students' concerns.

The involvement of LFI politicians has been documented by French media, although there is disagreement over whether the party helped initiate the demonstrations or became involved after the protests began.

An Oct. 2 investigation by Le Monde examined a police intelligence assessment describing radical left activity around schools in Seine-Saint-Denis but questioned whether the evidence established that the movement itself was politically orchestrated.
Feigenbaum offered a more cautious interpretation, describing some of the violent perpetrators as fringe provocateurs who exploit broader demonstrations without necessarily directing them.
"They're not being organized by some, you know, some mastermind at the national level, at least as far as anyone knows," he said.
FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE
Protesters hold Palestinian and Antifa flags as French high school and university students attend a demonstration in Strasbourg, France, Thursday, Oct. 6, 2026. (Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters)
Islamist influence or political solidarity?
The demonstrations have also raised questions about whether Islamist groups and pro-Palestinian activists are seeking to use the unrest to advance broader ideological causes.
Rodan-Benzaquen argued that Mélenchon's emphasis on Gaza and the Palestinian cause has helped bring together political constituencies that might otherwise have little in common.

"It's sort of the idea of sort of an intersection of different movements where they manage to bring together the different groups, the far left, Islamist movements, pro-Palestinian activists," she said.
She pointed to Palestinian flags appearing during the demonstrations as an indication of how the movement has expanded beyond its original educational demands.
The FDD expert argued that Islamist elements were attempting to capitalize on the turmoil, although she cautioned against reducing the entire crisis to immigration or religion.
"But this goes far beyond the issue of immigration. It goes far beyond the issue of Islamism. It goes far beyond the issue of Islam," she said.
EUROPE’S LEFT COURTS MUSLIM VOTERS AS ANTI-ISRAEL POLITICS RESHAPE CONTINENT
Students march with a large red banner reading "Police officers, enemy of the people" during a protest against under-resourced schools in Rennes, France, Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (Jeremias Gonzalez/AP)
A crisis France cannot simply spend its way out of
The government's latest concessions have not ended the protests.
According to Reuters on Friday, 141 schools remained closed while students continued demanding broader reforms. Nearly 10% of teaching hours in French public high schools remained unstaffed.
For Rodan-Benzaquen, one of the greatest dangers is that the demonstrations reflect a society increasingly divided into competing political realities.

She described how her 17-year-old son created separate left-wing and right-wing Instagram accounts and encountered radically different portrayals of the same unrest, one emphasizing police violence and the other violence by protesters.
"Now, if you live in two drastically different realities, it is very complicated to come to any form of dialog and end agreement," she said.
Her warning extends beyond France's current protests.
"We are in an extremely polarized environment," Rodan-Benzaquen said, noting that social media can deepen divisions and allow confrontations to escalate rapidly.
Feigenbaum sees an additional structural danger of a government burdened by accumulated financial obligations and deprived of the political consensus needed to reform them.

The result is a country spending heavily to sustain its public institutions while struggling to deliver the services citizens expect and a political system increasingly consumed by conflict over how to fix them.

French President Emmanuel Macron delivers a speech during the World Economic Forum annual meeting in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 20, 2026. (Harun Ozalp/Anadolu via Getty Images)

What began as a rebellion against broken classrooms has become a test of whether France can reconcile its costly promises with its financial reality before the divisions consuming its schools deepen further.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Massive 7.7 magnitude earthquake strikes Panama as officials investigate potential tsunami threat
summary: A powerful earthquake struck Panama's southern coast Friday, prompting officials to investigate a possible tsunami threat after the USGS lowered its magnitude estimate from 8.0 to 7.7.
story: Workers gathered in parks and public squares after a powerful earthquake shook buildings in Panama's capital Friday. (Credit: Associated Press)
A powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake struck off Panama's southern coast Friday, shaking the country's capital as officials investigated a potential tsunami threat.

The U.S. Geological Survey initially measured the earthquake at magnitude 8.0 before lowering its estimate to 7.7. The quake struck at 1:56 p.m. ET, at a depth of 7.8 miles, near Pitaloza Arriba, Panama.A 5.5 magnitude aftershock followed, with its epicenter approximately 50 miles east of the initial earthquake.The Panama Canal said operations were continuing normally following Friday's earthquake, with emergency protocols activated and technical teams inspecting facilities for possible damage. Canal officials said their priority was ensuring the safety of workers, vessels, crews and nearby communities as assessments continued.
MORE THAN 3,000 MISSING AFTER COLOMBIA EARTHQUAKE AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROVIDES $15.5 MILLION IN RELIEF
People stand outside the maternity ward of the Santo Tomas hospital after a severe magnitude 7.7 earthquake thet hit the country in Panama City Oct. 9, 2026. (Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty Images)
The earthquake was felt in Panama City and in San José, the capital of neighboring Costa Rica, according to Reuters.

Tsunami officials warned that waves reaching 3 to 10 feet above tide levels were possible along some coastal areas of Panama, while parts of Ecuador could experience waves of approximately 1 to 3 feet.
Smaller tsunami waves of less than 1 foot above tide levels were forecast for coastal areas of Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Nicaragua and Peru.
COLOMBIA BUILDING COLLAPSES ON CAMERA AS EARTHQUAKE BRINGS DEATH, DESTRUCTION
Medical workers and patients gather outside a hospital after a powerful earthquake in Panama Oct. 9, 2026. (Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty Images)
Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino said in a series of posts on X that he was visiting areas affected by Friday's earthquake and coordinating emergency assistance with government officials.

Mulino said he had ordered the mobilization of personnel, resources and aid for affected communities, along with structural assessments to determine the extent of the damage. He also thanked neighboring countries for their support and said assistance from the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean (CAF) would go toward helping those affected.
The president said he was traveling through Penonomé with government officials to coordinate relief efforts and thanked the United States and other countries for their offers of assistance.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a Friday post on X that the State Department was rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist Panama at the request of the Panamanian government. Rubio said the U.S. was closely monitoring the earthquake and directed Americans needing assistance to the department's 24-hour consular hotline at +1-202-501-4444 from abroad or +1-888-407-4747 from the U.S. and Canada.

The U.S. Embassy in Panama also said it was assessing potential damage and working to account for the safety and whereabouts of visitors and personnel. In a separate X post, the embassy urged Americans in Panama to enroll in the State Department's Smart Traveler Enrollment Program at STEP.State.gov and follow its social media accounts for updates.
Despite the potential danger to coastal communities near the earthquake, officials said a Pacific-wide tsunami was not expected.
People gather in a Panama City square after evacuating a building after a powerful earthquake. (Arnulfo Franco/AFP via Getty Images)
Earthquakes measuring between 7.0 and 7.9 can cause serious damage, according to Michigan Technological University.CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Information about possible damage or casualties from Friday's earthquake was not immediately available.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: DOJ threatens legal action against California over alleged noncitizen voters
summary: The DOJ demanded election officials review a list of possible noncitizens within 48 hours and “segregate” any mail ballots they sent in.
story: WASHINGTON — The Justice Department is threatening legal action against California unless state and local officials review a list of potential noncitizen individuals on their voter rolls.

Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter on Tuesday sent letters to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan with a list of names of possible noncitizens identified by the federal government. The letters demand they review the list by noon on Thursday.
“Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” McCotter wrote in the letters, which was obtained by NBC News.

McCotter wrote that the DOJ provided a password-protected thumb drive with a list of individuals the federal government “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot” for the 2026 election. He asked that county election officials “segregate — not cancel — those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots” until their citizenship status was determined.

“This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections,” a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement. “It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring.”
Reuters first reported on the letters.
Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor who was a Justice Department official during the Obama administration, said the federal government has no authority supporting its demands.
“They can send the letter,” he said. “California doesn’t have to do anything about it.”

Federal law prohibits systemic list maintenance within 90 days of a federal election. At this point, less than three weeks out from Election Day, the only changes to the voter rolls can come from individualized information, like notification from the Social Security Administration that someone has died.
A DOJ spokesperson said the department is asking California to sequester ballots, not change their voter list.

In a statement Wednesday, Logan said his office had not accessed the thumb drive the DOJ provided “because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.” He added, “We do not consider the device a secure medium.”

“Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office,” Logan said in the statement. “Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”
Weber said in a statement Wednesday that the DOJ did not provide a list of purported noncitizens to her office and that the administration lacked the legal authority for its request.

“The USDOJ’s relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said in the statement. “California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State’s voter rolls. My office and California election officials remain committed — as always — to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
All registered voters in California receive mail-in ballots, which started going out on Oct. 5.

The legal threats came amid a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizen individuals. Trump has long made unfounded claims that voting is marred by widespread fraud.
Election officials in several states — including Georgia, Connecticut, Nevada and Washington state — say they have received federal subpoenas in recent months for election records.
Some officials said they fear these actions were designed to set up possible legal challenges after the midterm elections.

“What we have seen is some groundwork laid out for postelection challenges,” said Stuart Holmes, the director of elections in Washington state. “Whether that’s the seizure of voting equipment, ballots themselves, tabulation equipment ... we’re preparing for any and all eventualities in that case.”

Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat, said officials in his state are also preparing for potential challenges to this November’s results. He added that he viewed the administration’s moves as “an effort to dissuade people from participating in the elections.”

“You have a president who’s trying to choose the voter base rather than the voters choosing the elected, and that’s not how our democracy works,” he said in an interview. “It’s the people control our elections, and when you try to take that control out, you do it through intimidation, you do it through threats, and you do it by trying to dissuade people from participating.”
Levitt agreed with the election officials’ conclusions.

“Are they laying the groundwork to say that voting was fraudulent? Of course they are, 100% they are,” he said, referring to the Trump administration. “Is the boy who cried wolf going to cry wolf? Yes, that’s what the boy who cried wolf does.”

Since Trump took office, his administration has brought over 100 cases involving allegations of voting by noncitizens. More than 154 million people voted in the 2024 election, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.
During the second Trump administration, the DOJ has sought voter registration data from every state in the country. It has filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing.

title: Suspicious white powder sent to election offices in 3 states
summary: No injuries or adverse health effects have been reported, and officials said they are working with state and federal law enforcement.
story: Secretaries of state’s offices in Ohio, Louisiana and Oklahoma were sent packages this week with mysterious powders, just weeks before the offices are set to oversee the midterm elections.
Oklahoma and Louisiana reported receiving the envelopes, while Ohio said U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a package destined for it.
The national groups representing secretaries of state and state election directors expressed concern about the suspicious letters in a letter Wednesday.

“As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement.
“Election officials take these matters seriously and work closely with law enforcement and security partners to protect their personnel and facilities,” the statement added.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose on Wednesday echoed the sentiment that election officials should “never have to fear for their personal safety while performing their duties,” adding that his office was working with state and federal law enforcement following the mailing targeting it.

“Fortunately, delivery of the letter was preempted by investigators at the U.S. Postal Service, who are dealing with similar mailings sent to election officials in multiple states,” LaRose said, while thanking the Postal Service.
For Subscribers
Ohio is one of a few states facing tight elections in just a few weeks.
The election bodies of Oklahoma and Louisiana, facing fewer contested elections, were threatened Tuesday, when each state announced it had received packages with suspicious powders.

“We want to assure Oklahoma voters that today’s incident does not impact our ability to conduct elections. Election officials remain committed to ensuring safe and secure elections,” Oklahoma State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax said in a statement.

Louisiana Secretary of State spokesperson Trey Williams said in an email Wednesday that an employee in the office’s Election Division opened a package containing a white powder and was taken uninjured to the emergency room “as a precaution.” Williams added that law enforcement did not find evidence of “harmful substances.”
For Subscribers
“Tuesday’s event did not impact any election operations in preparation for the upcoming election,” Williams said.
Louisiana State Police said in a statement that it responded to reports of a white powdery substance found in a package at the secretary of state’s office.

“LSP is working with the FBI to identify the substance, which was successfully recovered and submitted for testing at the FBI’s crime lab. No employees have reported injuries or adverse health effects related to the incident,” state police spokesperson Jacob Pucheu said in an emailed statement.
NBC affiliate KTAL of Shreveport reported Tuesday that the Baton Rouge building was evacuated.

The FBI declined in an email to confirm specific instances or locations. The agency said in a statement that it and the Postal Service were “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.”

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” the FBI’s national press office said.

It is not the first time that states’ election officials have faced threats near an election. In 2024, at least 20 states were targeted with letters containing suspicious powders. In one instance in Utah, a mailing with a suspicious powder was intercepted, with a letter signed by a so-called United States Traitor Elimination Army.
The mailings prompted several agencies, including the Justice Department, to release guidance about protecting personnel against hazardous materials.

title: Feds seized Rep. Ilhan Omar’s phone, subpoenaed family members in immigration status probe
summary: Federal agents seized the phone of Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., when they searched her Washington, D.C., home this week as part of a federal investigation into potential immigration-related crimes, and they have sent roughly a dozen subpoenas out in the case, according to two people familiar with the investigation.
story: Federal agents seized the phone of Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., when they searched her Washington, D.C., home this week as part of a federal investigation into potential immigration-related crimes, and they have sent roughly a dozen subpoenas out in the case, according to two people familiar with the investigation.
The possible charges cited by federal officials included conspiracy and making false statements in immigration paperwork, one of the people said.

The search came just three weeks before the midterms, within the window of time when the Justice Department has typically avoided overt actions in criminal cases that could affect an election. And the seizure of the phone of a sitting member of Congress would typically trigger a set of law enforcement protocols meant to ensure investigators aren’t infringing upon the “speech or debate” clause of the U.S. Constitution, which protects members of Congress from being questioned for their legislative acts.
On Friday, roughly a dozen subpoenas were sent out in the case, including to her family members, the second person familiar with the investigation told NBC News.

The congresswoman herself was not subpoenaed, the person said, adding that the orders seeking information are tied to a federal grand jury in Minnesota, Omar’s home state. Federal agents also want to talk to Omar’s sister but haven’t reached her yet, the person said.
The New York Times first reported the subpoenas.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The investigation is being conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, the U.S. attorney in Minneapolis and the Justice Department.
A spokesperson for Omar didn’t respond to a request for comment. The Justice Department declined to comment.
Omar said in a statement posted online on Monday that she would not be silenced.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she wrote.

One of the people familiar with the investigation said it involved whistleblowers, documents and witness testimony. The probe is examining matters surrounding Omar’s immigration status, including — but not limited to — her birthdate. Omar, who was born in Somalia and moved to the United States with her family in the 1990s, was naturalized when she was 17 years old, meaning she was a juvenile and could be conferred citizenship through a parent.

A criminal investigation could be complicated by the statute of limitations, which is typically five years, but investigators could look into Omar’s or her family members’ more recent actions that would fall within the statute of limitations.

Omar, who is part of a group of progressive women in Congress known as “the Squad,” has been a frequent target of Trump’s rhetoric against her and other members’ liberal positions, as well as Somali immigrants broadly.
Asked Monday if he had been aware of the search in advance, Trump said the federal government was looking at Omar “very carefully.” He also repeated his frequent attacks on her and Somalia.
“Then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution,” Trump said. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ.”
That evening, Trump also attacked Omar in remarks at a rally he held for Republicans in Ohio.

“I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: She’s a disaster,” Trump said. “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right.’”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appeared to tease federal action against Omar last month when he said “something’s going to happen” with her, but they were still investigating.

“If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case,” Mullin said. “It’s an actual case because they did things wrong. If you decided to break the law or lie [about] the information you gave the United States to be able to come into the United States through either asylum or because you were just wanting to seek a better life, but you didn’t tell us who you actually were, you lied about certain things about your application — those things, there’s no expiration to that.”

title: Romance scammers are getting harder to catch. The consequences are costly.
summary: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.
story: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.

A congressional investigation, which began in September 2025 and lasted about a year, found that Tinder’s scam detection systems struggled for years to keep fraudulent accounts off the dating app. Parent company Match Group has since moved to address the shortcomings with new verification requirements and upgraded detection technology.
Romance scams have become a leading form of financial fraud in the U.S., costing Americans nearly $1.5 billion in reported losses last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

“There’s a lot of stigma to being a victim to scams,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who launched the investigation alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in an interview last week. “People should understand that really sophisticated people who are doing all the right things are still getting scammed because of the level of technology and resources that these criminal enterprises now do.”

Scammers today can realistically pose as representatives from familiar organizations like the local YMCA or a bank, and the accessibility of AI tools makes it easier than ever to research family members and mimic their voices. But romance scams, Hassan said, can be particularly emotionally devastating.

That was the case for Pennsylvania resident Sue Nuss, who told Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship after she lost her husband. There, she met a man who claimed to be from New Jersey.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.
-Sue nuss, who spoke to Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship.
Nuss told NBC News that, over a month and a half, he won her trust with words that made her feel like he really “sees” and “understands” her.

The committee’s report, published Tuesday, stated that the man duped Nuss with a series of “fabricated” crises: job problems on an oil rig, an arrest in Mexico, his mom’s stroke and even her funeral — all excuses to ask Nuss, 77, for money. When the scammers behind the profile tried to trick her into believing the man she was dating had died, she said, she realized it was all a scam.

“I have always been a very giving person my entire life, and I’ve always been a caregiver,” Nuss told NBC News last week. “And I fell prey. I was very vulnerable. I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.”
Days after what she thought was a budding online relationship fell apart, Nuss’ scammer showed back up on Tinder with the same profile, she said in an interview.

Soon, another group approached her claiming they could recover what she had lost. Then, through an elaborate cryptocurrency scheme, that group managed to scam even more money from Nuss. She believes both scammer groups were connected, the report stated. It added that, in total, she lost more than $700,000.

“I struggle. Some days are really bad days and some days are good days. I do get therapy. I’m starting a very special therapy next week called EMDR because it’s a trauma,” Nuss said. “I don’t trust my decisions now.”

Congress last month passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which would require online dating service providers to notify and warn any users who get messaged by potential scammers. The bill awaits President Donald Trump’s signature.

This summer, Hassan also introduced legislation with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., to create a central reporting portal for victims of scams, an initiative that she said could give the federal government the tools to detect patterns in scams to shut them down more effectively.
Scammers stole more than $1 trillion globally in one year, according to a 2024 report from the Global Anti-Scam Alliance.

“Enterprises that run scams are now costing the global economy more than the illicit drug trade does,” Hassan said. “This is really important for individuals. It’s really important for our economy. And so, the more people speak up about the need to change the way the federal government handles scams, the faster it’s going to happen.”

The Joint Economic Committee’s investigation sought to combat the prevalence of romance scams on platforms owned by Match Group, the biggest online dating company in the world, with a portfolio that includes Tinder, Hinge, Match and Plenty of Fish.

It found that during the first nine months of 2025, nearly 1.5 million scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with someone. Nearly 500,000 of those accounts then exchanged contact information with other users.

Internal documents shared voluntarily with the committee noted that most of Tinder’s machine-learning detection scam models hadn’t been updated in years, and Match Group staff members found that scammers could quickly circumvent the company’s patchwork detection rules. Excessive false positives also overwhelmed the human moderators trying to detect dangerous accounts.
The committee wrote that it welcomes the changes Match Group has made to address those concerns.

Match Group deployed new detection models throughout the latter half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 to better catch bad actors, according to the committee’s report. This year, it introduced 169 automated rules and “improved” 108 others aimed at targeting and removing inauthentic actors.

One of its key rollouts is a mandatory biometric face check for all new users on Tinder and Hinge, meant to prevent users from making multiple accounts and ensure banned users can’t make new accounts.

Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice president of trust and safety, told NBC News the company is “grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.”

“That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history,” Roth wrote in a statement. “Trust and Safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.”

Much of that safety work, including the face checks, was already underway before the committee’s investigation, according to Match Group. It reports having seen a roughly 60% reduction in exposure to bad actors in every market since the face checks began.
Hassan similarly said those measures have “already been successful in dramatically reducing the number of matches that their customers have with a scammer.”

“They need to do more, though, because there are still gaps in their systems,” she added. “And they are going to need to stay vigilant in new ways, because the criminals are always changing their technology and their tactics, too.”

title: Prosecutors seeking life sentences for real estate brokers, brother convicted of sex trafficking
summary: Oren, Alon and Tal Alexander were convicted in April of running a sex trafficking ring, with prosecutors accusing them of using drugs and their influence to sexually abuse women.
story: Federal prosecutors in New York are seeking life sentences for two former luxury real estate brokers and their brother, who were convicted this year of using their influence to drug and sexually abuse women over several years, according to court documents.

Twins Oren and Alon Alexander and their brother Tal “have been convicted of sex crimes of extraordinary magnitude,” prosecutors with the U.S. attorney’s office in Manhattan wrote in a sentencing memorandum filed Wednesday.

“They spent years designing, executing, and perfecting their playbook of luring victims with promises of luxury, drugging victims so they could not resist, and then forcibly raping them,” prosecutors wrote.

The brothers were found guilty of 10 counts of engaging in a yearslong conspiracy of rape, sex trafficking, sex abuse and sexual exploitation. They pleaded not guilty but were convicted in April after a trial in which 11 accusers testified.
One accuser testified that Alon Alexander drugged and raped her after a night out at a New York City club. She told the court that after she was given a drink, her “body started to sway.”
She testified that she woke up naked on a bed with Alon Alexander, who did not have any clothes on, standing over her.

“I tried to get out of the bed a few times, but Alon kept pushing me back down,” she said. “Finally, he sat down on the bed, and I was able to get up, and I said, ‘I don’t want to have sex with you,’ and he said, ‘You already did.’”
Oren and Tal Alexander were powerful luxury real estate brokers. Prosecutors said the brothers used their wealth and influence to prey on women and coerce them into sex acts.
In arguing for a life sentence, prosecutors wrote in Wednesday’s filing that over 70 women came forward with “harrowing accounts of assault that stripped them of their dignity and autonomy.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Attorneys for the brothers said in a sentencing submission filed Tuesday that the brothers are innocent.
The brothers will each ask for a sentence of 15 years, the defense attorneys wrote, which is the minimum sentence under some of the charges of which they were convicted.

The defense attorneys wrote that all three brothers were competitive with one another and others when it came to dating women and that in the years before they were charged, “they engaged in conduct that was, at times, insensitive toward the feelings of certain women.”
“But Alon, Oren and Tal steadfastly maintain their complete innocence of these awful charges,” the defense attorneys wrote. “At no time did Alon, Oren or Tal rape or sexually assault another person.”
Sentencing is set for Oct. 27.

title: Advocates fear deportation of potential witnesses in back of ICE vehicle that hit Houston man
summary: Nidia Delfín said her brother was handcuffed in the back of the ICE vehicle when it hit a man, adding that he has no arrest warrants and that he was getting his green card when he was arrested.
story: HOUSTON — Two handcuffed men were in the backseat of an ICE vehicle Saturday when it struck and injured Miguel Parra Hernandez as he fled on foot in Houston.
Advocates are fighting to make sure the men — now potential witnesses — are not deported.
At a news conference Wednesday, family members, advocates and attorneys identified one of the men as Luis Delfín Enríquez, 48.
Video appears to show Houston man run over by ICE vehicle

Nidia Delfín, Delfín’s sister, said her brother was handcuffed in the backseat of the ICE vehicle when it hit Parra, adding that he was on his way to breakfast with employees when he was apprehended by ICE. She said that Delfín is not a criminal, that he has no arrest warrants and that he was in the process of getting his green card, which means he was on the path to being a legal permanent resident.
“He owns his own small company. He hires people from the community. He is a good man,” she said, adding that he witnessed “this horrific incident.”

She said that she, her parents and her brother are afraid but that they are speaking up so Parra “can get justice.” She pleaded with others in the community who witnessed the incident — she said she has seen videos on social media — to do the same and share the information they have.
“What was done to him is not OK,” she said, referring to Parra. “It’s not how we’re supposed to treat other human beings.”

Cesar Espinosa of FIEL Houston, an immigrant civil rights organization who is representing Parra’s family, said the men held in the ICE vehicle “witnessed everything that happened,” including “the moment when Mr. Miguel [Parra] was run over.”

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News on Tuesday that videos gathered by his office suggest that Parra was struck intentionally. Teare said his office is seeking to interview the witnesses as it investigates the case.
“This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said.

A senior Department of Homeland Security official told NBC News on Tuesday that ICE officers on the scene were wearing body cameras and that the agency is reviewing video for an internal investigation.
ICE has said allegations that the agency intentionally struck Parra are “RECKLESS and FALSE.”
Espinosa said that if there is video from body cameras, it should be turned over to the district attorney’s office immediately.

A government watchdog report released Wednesday found that Customs and Border Protection and ICE have not developed specific operational guidance to explain how their personnel should use body cameras.
Without that guidance, “CBP and ICE personnel will fail to use the cameras as required under policy,” the Government Accountability Office said in its report.
The Trump administration issued guidance two weeks ago that dictated that officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

DHS and ICE did not immediately respond to questions about the release of the bodycam video, whether they planned to deport witnesses to the incident and the status of the ICE officer who drove the vehicle that hit Parra.

Security video of the incident obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. Parra and another man exit the white truck and run, the video shows.
At about the same time, the video shows, another vehicle jumps a yellow median and heads in Parra’s direction.

The video then shows the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. When the parked truck leaves, a man can be seen lying on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.
Teare, a Democrat, told NBC News the investigation could lead to charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.

Espinosa said at the news conference that Parra does not feel safe at the hospital. The ICE officers who were there when he was struck “are the same crew that are watching him 24/7” at the hospital, Espinosa said. He did not know whether the driver of the vehicle was among those guarding Parra.
ICE did not immediately confirm whether the ICE officers involved in Saturday’s incident are with Parra at the hospital.
Espinosa, Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno and Parra’s family demanded at the news conference that ICE keep Parra at the hospital where he is being treated for his multiple injuries.
Without the proper medical care, he could end up with infections and other problems that could be life-threatening, “so we need him to get the best medical care possible,” Espinosa said.

Espinosa and Bruno said Parra still has not been processed by ICE, which has said that he is in the country illegally. Bruno and Espinosa confirmed that Parra was undocumented and said they could not provide further information about whether he was seeking other status.
Parra, who works applying stucco, has been in the country 34 years, having arrived at age 14, Espinosa and Bruno said.
The man who was driving the truck with Parra and also ran away was identified at the news conference as “Omar.” He does not have a criminal record or any open immigration warrants, Espinosa said.
At the news conference, advocates criticized ICE for pursuing Parra with the immigrants handcuffed in their car, endangering everyone, according to Espinosa.
Teare, who served several years as the chief of the district attorney’s vehicular crimes division, also criticized ICE’s tactics.
“The behavior of this agency and these agents on our streets is so dangerous to everyone that lives in these communities,” he said in an interview Tuesday.
ICE did not immediately respond to allegations that it was conducting an immigration stop while it was transporting immigrants it had previously apprehended.
ICE has said in statements that it was pursuing a man it identified as Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. It has said Parra was not its target.

Espinosa repeatedly held up a photo of Mendoza at the news conference and said no one, including Parra, recognized him or knew who he was. He also showed a photo of Omar, the man who was with Parra in the car before they fled, to show it was not Mendoza.
“If he [Mendoza] does exist, he must be taken into custody, and a proper thorough investigation must be done so that he may be looked at,” Espinosa said.

title: Trump says government officials who leak to the media ‘should be shot’
summary: The administration has repeatedly sought to crack down on information leaks to the media.
story: President Donald Trump said at a campaign rally Wednesday that there should be fatal consequences for any government worker who leaks sensitive information to the media.
“Leakers should be, in my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump said. “You know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”

Trump described what he said was a planned raid on Iran that he had to call off after someone “leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving.” He appeared to be referring to the U.S. military strike on Iran nuclear facilities in June 2025, which still went ahead.
Trump says leakers 'should be shot'

“Somebody leaked, some sleazebag. They ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail, but they leaked that we were leaving at 12:07 from Missouri, and it was in The New York Times, CNN.”
“Now, the leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly. They’re real. To me, they’re the scum of the Earth,” he said.
Trump, who has called the news media the “true Enemy of the People,” then pointed to the journalists covering his rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, and compared them to leakers.
“Those same people up there, they’re almost as bad as a leaker, because they leak,” Trump said. “Oh, they leak false information. That makes them a leaker, right?”

Since Trump returned to office, his administration has sought to crack down on information leaked to the media, including proposing to direct federal agencies to have “new and existing employees” sign nondisclosure agreements.

Federal investigators subjected about 50 members of the U.S. military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests, pressing them about whether they had shared classified information with journalists, the Times reported last month, citing officials briefed on the move.

In January, Trump authorized a search of the home of Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson as part of an investigation into a government contractor who was accused of illegally retaining classified materials. A federal magistrate judge ruled a month later that the administration could not examine the data that FBI agents had seized there. The administration appealed the ruling, but it was upheld by a district court judge. There have been no further appeals.

In June, the administration tried to compel testimony from four journalists, three from the Post and one from The Wall Street Journal, before a grand jury, an official familiar with the matter told NBC News at the time. The administration dropped the subpoenas after newspapers pushed back.

title: Kentucky police arrest 8 in child abuse, trafficking and rape case
summary: The seven victims are ages 1 to 17, police in Richmond said.
story: Eight people living in a Kentucky home were arrested in a sweeping child abuse and sexual abuse case involving seven victims, ages 1 to 17, officials said Wednesday.

The suspects face a slew of charges, including abuse, incest, human trafficking and rape. Bail has been set at $50,000 to $125,000, Richmond police spokesperson Makenzie Gould told NBC News in a statement.
All eight defendants are scheduled to appear before a Madison County judge on Oct. 21.
For Subscribers
The arrests followed a joint investigation by Richmond police, Child Protective Services and the Department for Community Based Services, police said in a statement.
“I’m unsure of the exact family relations between all eight members,” Gould said. “All are listed as living at the same residence. All seven children were removed from this same residence.”
